capabilities.name: Autoplay audio and video
capabilities.plain: Starts video or sound automatically; muted video is allowed, sound usually needs prior interaction.
capabilities.meaning: A site can start media without a click. Browsers allow silent autoplay but block surprise sound unless the person has engaged with the site, which shapes ad video and background audio.

limits.headline: Can start muted video on its own, and sound only after you have interacted
limits.user_action: Nothing for muted video. For sound, you tap, click or press a key on the site first
can: Start a silent video without a click
Start sound after you have clicked, tapped or watched on the site
Start a clip after you tap Play
cannot: Play sound on a first visit without any interaction
Keep a sound ad alive in a tab you muted
Override your browser's autoplay setting
Play a video in the background once the page is hidden on most phones
limits.reach_label: Muted video, sound after you interact
limits.differs: Safari and iPhone are strict about sound. Chrome and Edge allow sound for sites you used often. Firefox lets you block it.

story.what_it_is: A page can start video or sound by itself. Muted video is usually fine, sound needs your action first.

marketing.name: Autoplay policy
marketing.pitch: Chrome allows muted autoplay, and lets sound autoplay only after you have interacted with the site.

marketing.name: New video policies for iOS
marketing.pitch: Safari lets muted videos play inline automatically, and requires a tap for videos with sound.

story.for_you: A video on a page may start playing silently as you scroll. Sound normally starts only after you click or tap. Browsers keep this rule to avoid surprise noise.
story.for_makers: Makers use muted autoplay to show previews and grab attention, which raises views and ad time. They ask for a tap before sound. Games need one click before audio. Ads that autoplay can annoy users.

use_cases.example: A streaming home page plays a silent trailer behind the title, so browsing feels alive.
A browser game must wait for your first click or key press before its music and sounds can play.
A social feed starts muted clips as you scroll, and you tap to hear them.
A news site starts a muted video in an article, which many people watch with captions.
A video ad starts muted in the page, and counts a view after a few seconds.
A store plays a muted product video on the page to show the item in use.
A live stream page starts muted and asks you to unmute for sound.
A music site shows a play button, because the browser blocks sound until you tap.

technical_bounds: Muted autoplay is allowed everywhere (iOS also needs playsinline)
Chrome 66: audible autoplay needs user activation on the origin, a high MEI score, or an installed PWA; MEI needs roughly 20 visits and a score of about 0.2 to 0.3 (Chromium source)
MEI counts a play as significant when media plays 7 s or more, is audible, tab active, and video at least 200 by 140 px
Firefox 66 blocks audible autoplay by default (site exceptions allowed); Safari 11 on macOS and iOS 10 block audible autoplay by default
Chrome mutes autoplay in cross-origin iframes unless allow="autoplay" is set

history.change: Block audible autoplay by default on macOS
Autoplay policy: muted allowed; audible needs activation, MEI or PWA
Autoplay policy for media in background tabs unchanged; play() promise rejection documented widely

refs.label: WebKit new video policies for iOS

platform.api: <video autoplay muted playsinline>; HTMLMediaElement.play(); allow="autoplay"; navigator.getAutoplayPolicy()

access.persistence: Chrome Media Engagement Index (MEI) score is stored per origin
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Top frame must delegate with allow="autoplay" for cross-origin iframes
steps: Element has muted attribute or origin has activation or high MEI
play() resolves or rejects with NotAllowedError
Handle the rejection and show a play button

capabilities.name: Leave-page confirmation (beforeunload)
capabilities.plain: Shows a generic Leave site? dialog, only if the person interacted with the page.
capabilities.meaning: A site can ask the person to confirm closing or leaving, often to protect unsaved work. Browsers hide the site's own text, so it cannot scare people with custom messages.

limits.headline: Can show a generic Leave site? warning when you close or leave, after you have interacted
limits.user_action: You click, tap or type on the page, then try to close or leave it
can: Show a Leave site? box to protect your unsaved work
Show it when you close the tab or window
Show it when you press back or go to another site
cannot: Show custom text, since browsers hide the site's own message
Show the box if you have not touched the page
Block you for good, since you can still leave
Work on iPhone browsers
limits.differs: Works in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari on computers. iPhone browsers do not show it.

story.what_it_is: A page can show a generic Are you sure you want to leave dialog, only after you used the page.

marketing.name: beforeunload event
marketing.pitch: Lets a page warn before you leave, with a standard message, only if you have interacted with it.

story.for_you: If you try to close a page with unsaved work, a box asks Leave site? You can stay or leave. Pages you never touched cannot show it.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to protect unsaved work in forms, editors and checkouts. Browsers use a fixed message to stop it being used to trap people. Misuse by scam sites is limited by the click rule.

use_cases.example: A web editor like Google Docs warns you if edits are not saved yet when you close the tab.
A checkout page asks if you want to leave with items in your cart and a half filled form.
A browser game asks before you leave a ranked match where leaving counts as a loss.
A web design tool warns about unsynced changes.
A test platform warns a student before they close an exam.
A bank page warns you before you leave a half finished transfer.
A scam page tries to trap you with repeated Leave prompts, but browsers allow it only after you click.

technical_bounds: Needs sticky user activation: no dialog if the page was never clicked or typed in (Chrome 60)
Custom message text is ignored (Chrome 51, Firefox 44, Safari 9.1)
Cannot run async work or block navigation indefinitely: dialog is the only block
A beforeunload listener makes a page ineligible for the back/forward cache in Chrome desktop and Firefox
Not reliable on mobile: tab discard and app switch skip it; use pagehide and visibilitychange

history.change: Dialog requires user interaction with the page

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Fires on each unload attempt while the listener exists
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Dialog suppressed in cross-origin iframes without activation
steps: Person interacts with the page (sticky activation)
Page registers beforeunload and sets returnValue
On close or navigate, browser shows generic confirmation

capabilities.name: Compression Streams
capabilities.plain: Compresses or decompresses data in the page with built-in gzip, deflate or deflate-raw.
capabilities.meaning: A site can shrink or expand data without a library. It also lets trackers pack fingerprint payloads before sending them out.

limits.headline: Can squeeze or unpack data in the page with the browser's built in compression
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a site's script compresses logs, files or data
can: Compress data with gzip or deflate before sending it
Unpack compressed files in the page
Shrink payloads, including tracking data, before they go out
cannot: See your files unless you chose them
Send anything by itself, only change data the page already has
Be turned off from your browser settings
Do heavy work forever, since large tricks can hit memory limits

story.what_it_is: A page can squeeze or unpack data with built in compression, so it sends less over the network.

marketing.name: Compression Streams API
marketing.pitch: Gives pages fast built in gzip and deflate, with no extra code to download.

story.for_you: You never see it. Pages that use it send smaller uploads and open big files faster. It saves time and data.
story.for_makers: Makers drop heavy compression libraries and ship less code. It speeds up uploads, saves and downloads. The same trick can hide the size of data a script sends out, which tracking code can use.

use_cases.example: A browser game compresses save files before uploading them to the cloud, so saves are quick on mobile data.
A web editor compresses documents before sync and saves bandwidth.
A web design tool unpacks large project files in the browser.
A web video app packs frames or clips before an upload.
An analytics script compresses batches of events before sending them in one request.
A web tool lets you drag in a zip or gzip file and view its contents in the page.
A tracking script packs a large fingerprint into a small request that is hard to spot.

technical_bounds: Formats: gzip, deflate, deflate-raw (brotli not in the spec baseline)
Streaming only, no password or zip container; browser does not compress files on disk
DecompressionStream has no output cap; zip bomb risk fills memory
Support: Chrome 80, Safari 16.4, Firefox 113

abuse: Memory exhaustion with a decompression bomb

access.persistence: None
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag; available in workers

capabilities.name: Cookie Store API
capabilities.plain: Reads and changes cookies asynchronously and gets change events, including in service workers.
capabilities.meaning: A site can watch and edit its own cookies without parsing document.cookie. It sees only non-HttpOnly cookies for its own origin.

limits.headline: Can watch and change the site's own cookies, but not hidden ones or other sites' cookies
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the site's script checks or sets a cookie
can: List and change the site's own cookies that scripts may see
Get a notice when its own cookies change, including in a background script
Keep your sign in in step across tabs
cannot: See other sites' cookies
See protected cookies marked HttpOnly
Work from outside the site's own address
Be sure to stop cookie syncing, which you stop by clearing cookies or blocking trackers

story.what_it_is: A page can read and change cookies the modern way and hear about changes, even in background scripts.

marketing.name: Cookie Store API
marketing.pitch: Offers an async way to read and write cookies and to listen for changes, including in service workers.

story.for_you: You never see it. Sites use it to remember your login and settings. If you clear cookies, the site will see the change.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to manage login, consent choices and tracking IDs without blocking the page. Change events let them react when cookies are added or cleared. It works inside background scripts too.

use_cases.example: A store keeps your cart and login in cookies, and notices if they are cleared to rebuild your session.
An ad script watches for cookie changes and re-creates its ID if you clear it.
An analytics tool reads and writes its visitor ID cookie, and sends a new event when it changes.
A browser game portal stores your sign in and settings in cookies, and syncs across tabs.
A bank page detects when its session cookie is removed and logs out the tab.
A news site stores your cookie consent choices and reads them in the background scripts.
A streaming site shares a login across tabs using cookie change events.

technical_bounds: HTTPS only; cannot read HttpOnly cookies
Cookie size limit 4096 bytes for name plus value; about 180 cookies per domain in Chrome, 50 per domain in Firefox (older), 150 in Safari
Max Expires/Max-Age cap is 400 days in Chrome (Chrome 104)
Third-party contexts follow normal third-party cookie blocking and the Storage Access API
Support per MDN BCD: Chrome and Edge 87, Safari 18.4, Firefox 140

history.change: Cookie Max-Age and Expires capped at 400 days
Cookie Store API ships in Safari
Cookie Store API ships in Firefox

platform.api: cookieStore.get(), getAll(), set(), delete(); cookiechange event

access.persistence: Same as the cookie lifetime
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-origin and secure contexts only
steps: cookiechange event fires in other tabs and service workers

capabilities.name: Cross-origin isolation (SharedArrayBuffer, COOP, COEP)
capabilities.plain: A site can opt into an isolated mode that unlocks SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers and Wasm threads.
capabilities.meaning: Isolation trades openness (no cross-origin popups or unmarked embeds) for power. Sites with it get memory sharing and 5 microsecond timers, which are also better side channel tools.

limits.headline: Can switch on a locked down mode that unlocks fast shared memory for the page
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the site loads with the right security headers set.
can: Share memory between background threads for heavy apps like games and editors
Run the page's own code with very precise timers
Start multi threaded compiled code inside the page
cannot: Open popups that stay linked to other sites while isolation is on
Load embedded videos, ads or widgets that are not marked to allow it
Turn itself on without the site's own server sending the right headers
See anything in other tabs or other sites
limits.differs: Works in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, including on iPhone and Android.

story.what_it_is: A site can switch on a locked down mode that unlocks very fast, shared memory tricks.

marketing.name: Cross-origin isolation
marketing.pitch: Chrome's web.dev guide says isolation unlocks powerful features like SharedArrayBuffer and high precision timers, in exchange for stricter rules about embeds.

story.for_you: You never see a prompt. A big web app just runs smoother, but some embedded widgets, like a video or ad frame, may refuse to load until their owners add the right labels.
story.for_makers: Makers flip this on to get shared memory and multi threaded compiled code, which game engines and heavy editors need. The cost is that every third party embed on the page must opt in too, which is a real project for ad heavy sites.

use_cases.example: A Unity or Unreal game exported to the browser uses several worker threads at once, which only works when the page is isolated.
A web video editor trims and renders clips using many CPU threads so the preview stays smooth.
Spreadsheets and CAD tools in the browser share one big block of memory between workers to crunch numbers faster.
An in browser coding sandbox runs a whole Node style environment and needs shared memory to do it.
Security teams use isolation to make sure that a page cannot be read by other sites' scripts, a defence against Spectre style attacks.
Ad networks must retag their frames and scripts so a publisher can turn isolation on without breaking ad slots.

technical_bounds: SharedArrayBuffer requires crossOriginIsolated (Chrome 92, Firefox 79, Safari 15.2)
COEP require-corp: every subresource needs CORP or CORS; credentialless mode available in Chrome 96 and Firefox 119
COOP same-origin severs window.opener to cross-origin popups (breaks OAuth popups unless same-origin-allow-popups)
Isolated pages get performance.now at 5 microsecond resolution (Chrome) instead of 100 microseconds
Chrome on Android got SharedArrayBuffer under the same rule in 92

abuse: Fast timer side channels (Spectre style) if isolation fails

platform.api: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin; Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp or credentialless; self.crossOriginIsolated

access.persistence: Set per document via headers
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Embedded frames need CORP or CORS (require-corp) or credentialless mode
steps: Server sends COOP and COEP headers
SharedArrayBuffer and fine timers become available

capabilities.name: alert, confirm and prompt dialogs
capabilities.plain: Blocks the page with a modal alert, confirm or prompt box.
capabilities.meaning: A site can interrupt the person with a message or a text box. Dialogs freeze the page script, are easy to abuse, and are blocked in cross-origin iframes and background tabs.

limits.headline: Can freeze the page with a pop up message box until you answer it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page runs a script, or after an action like Delete.
can: Show an alert, a yes or no question or a box asking you to type text
Pause the page until you tap OK or Cancel
Ask Are you sure you want to leave? before you close the tab
cannot: Show the box on tabs you are not looking at in most browsers
Pause other tabs or other apps
Fill your screen with endless boxes; browsers let you block more from that page
See what you type into other sites
limits.reach_label: One page, one box at a time

story.what_it_is: A site can pop up a message box that freezes the page until you click.
story.for_you: You see a grey box that says something like 'Leave site?' or 'Are you sure?' and the page stops until you answer. Scam sites use fake versions to scare you.
story.for_makers: Makers use these for the simplest possible yes or no and for quick debugging. Browsers now limit them, so serious apps build their own dialogs instead.

use_cases.example: An online editor asks 'Discard unsaved changes?' when you try to close the tab.
A checkout page asks 'Are you sure you want to leave? Your cart will be lost.'
A fake 'Your computer is infected, call this number' alert loops on a scam site until you force quit.
A developer drops quick alert boxes into code to see a value while testing.
A simple browser game confirms 'Restart level?' before wiping your progress.
An old internal admin tool asks 'Delete 40 records?' with a plain browser confirm box.

technical_bounds: Cross-origin iframe dialogs are blocked in Chrome 92 (and Safari, Firefox have similar restrictions); same-origin iframes still allowed
Dialogs from background tabs are queued until the tab is foregrounded in Chrome
Chrome shows a Prevent this page from creating more dialogs checkbox on repeated dialogs
Dialog text is plain text, no HTML; Chrome shows the origin in the title
Modal blocks the whole event loop of the tab (and other same-process tabs may freeze)

abuse: Dialog loops that trap the tab

history.change: Cross-origin iframe alert, confirm, prompt blocked
Dialog from background tab queued; tab-modal dialogs introduced earlier

access.persistence: One-shot; Chrome adds Prevent this page from creating more dialogs after repeats
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Blocked in cross-origin iframes in Chrome 92 and later; sandboxed frames need allow-modals
steps: Browser shows modal dialog and blocks the page thread
Return value goes back to script

capabilities.name: Trigger file downloads
capabilities.plain: Saves a file to the device; repeated automatic downloads ask permission.
capabilities.meaning: A site can drop files into Downloads (reports, exports, installers). Browsers guard with multi-download prompts and safe browsing checks because a downloaded file is how malware arrives.

limits.headline: Can save a file to your device, but repeated automatic downloads ask first
limits.user_action: Nothing for the first one. It happens when the page runs a download or you tap a link.
can: Save a file to your Downloads folder when you tap a download link
Make a file on the spot, such as a receipt or a report, and save it
Start one download without asking in most browsers
cannot: Save many files in a row without a second prompt asking you to allow it
Open or run the file for you; you still have to open it
Save the file anywhere except the browser's download location
Skip the browser's warning for risky file types
limits.reach_label: One file, then it asks again
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox ask before several automatic downloads. Safari on iPhone shows a download button for each file.

story.what_it_is: A site can save a file to your device, and the browser asks if it keeps doing it.
story.for_you: You click a button and a file lands in your Downloads folder. If a page tries to download many files by itself, the browser asks whether to allow that.
story.for_makers: Makers build files in the page (a report, an image, an export) and hand them over with one click. It saves server work and lets apps feel like desktop programs.

use_cases.example: You hit Export on a spreadsheet web app and it makes the CSV file right inside your browser.
A design tool saves your finished artwork as a PNG or PDF straight from the page.
Your bank offers a statement as a PDF download for your tax records.
A browser game lets you download your save file so you can move it to another computer.
A malicious site tries to push a file you did not ask for, which is why browsers warn on repeated automatic downloads.
A web video editor renders your clip and downloads the MP4 when it is done.

technical_bounds: download attribute is ignored for cross-origin URLs (Chrome 65, Firefox); filename comes from the response then
Second and later downloads without a click trigger Chrome's Automatic downloads prompt (Firefox shows a similar download panel)
Chrome blocks downloads from sandboxed iframes without allow-downloads (Chrome 83) and insecure (HTTP) downloads on HTTPS pages (Chrome 86 to 88)
Cannot choose the download folder; cannot open the file; dangerous file types get a warning
Blob URLs and data: URIs for large files are limited by memory (Chrome about 2 GB single Blob); stream with FSA or Streams for bigger files

history.change: download attribute ignored for cross-origin URLs
Downloads in sandboxed iframes need allow-downloads
Mixed-content downloads blocked in phases (executables first in Chrome 88)

refs.label: Chrome download restrictions in sandboxed iframes

access.persistence: Chrome stores Automatic downloads permission per origin after the person allows it
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Sandboxed frames need allow-downloads (Chrome 83); downloads from cross-origin iframes without activation are blocked
steps: Page creates anchor or sends Content-Disposition
Safe Browsing may warn or block

capabilities.name: Drag and drop
capabilities.plain: Lets people drag items within or into the page, and lets the page start drags.
capabilities.meaning: A site can start a drag with text, links or files, and react when people drop things on it. Data in a drag is readable only on drop, so the page cannot spy on a drag it does not own.

limits.headline: Can let you drag items on the page, or drop files onto it
limits.user_action: You drag a file, text or picture onto the page, or drag an item inside it.
can: Accept files you drop onto the page, such as photos or documents
Let you rearrange items by dragging, like cards or lists
Start a drag so you can pull text or an image out of the page
cannot: See your files before you drop them
See files you did not drop
Browse your folders on its own
Take over dragging from other apps or windows

story.what_it_is: People can drag things around the page, or drop files onto it.

marketing.name: HTML Drag and Drop API
marketing.pitch: MDN explains that pages can make items draggable and react when you drop files or text on them.

story.for_you: You pick up a card, a file or a photo with your mouse or finger and drop it somewhere else. It feels natural, so you rarely think about it.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to make web apps feel like real software: reordering lists, uploading by dropping a file, building layouts. It also boosts upload completion because dropping is easier than browsing folders.

use_cases.example: You drag a task card from To Do to Done in a project board.
You drop a photo onto a design canvas and it appears where you let go.
You drag pieces on a browser puzzle or card game, like moving a card in solitaire.
You drag a file into a chat window to send it.
You drag songs into a playlist order on a web music player.
You drag a product into a wish list or onto a compare bar.

risks: Dropped files read by the page

technical_bounds: dataTransfer is in protected mode outside drop: types are visible, data is not readable until drop
Cannot start an OS file drag from the page except the Chrome only DownloadURL type trick
Dropped files expose name, size, type, lastModified; no full path
Touch support: iOS Safari 11 (iPad and iPhone); Android Chrome supports long-press drag since Chrome 96 on some devices
Drag image limited to a rendered element or image; size capped by the OS

abuse: Exfil of dropped sensitive files into the wrong site

history.change: Touch drag and drop on iOS 11 and iPadOS

refs.label: MDN HTML Drag and Drop API

platform.api: dragstart, dragover, drop events; DataTransfer; draggable=true

access.persistence: Per drag operation
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Dragging across iframes allowed; dropped data readable only in the drop handler
steps: Person drags an item over the page
dragover must call preventDefault to accept

capabilities.name: Fenced frames
capabilities.plain: Embeds content that cannot talk to or be read by the page around it.
capabilities.meaning: Used by ad auctions so the embedding page cannot see which ad rendered. It separates the frame's storage and messaging from the parent to block link-back tracking.

limits.headline: Can embed a box of content that the page around it cannot look into
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, usually where an ad or a widget sits.
can: Show an ad or widget inside the page
Keep the embedded content walled off from the host site
Let ad systems pick an ad without sharing your details with the page
cannot: Share what is inside the box with the page around it
Send scrolling or clicks to the host site beyond what the rules allow
Work in Firefox or Safari, including on iPhone
Be used by every site yet; it is still limited and new
limits.reach_label: A sealed box inside the page
limits.differs: Only Chrome based browsers support it today. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: A box inside a page that is sealed off, so neither side can read the other.

marketing.name: Fenced Frame
marketing.pitch: Chrome's Privacy Sandbox docs describe it as a frame that can show content without sharing information with the embedding page.

story.for_you: You see an ad or embed as normal. What you cannot see is that the page around it is blocked from learning which ad it is, which was meant to stop sites linking your browsing across pages.
story.for_makers: It lets ad tech pick an ad using your interests without handing your identity to the publisher. Advertisers still get counts of views and clicks through special reports, so measurement stays alive.

use_cases.example: An interest based ad is chosen in your browser and shown in a sealed frame, so the news site cannot see which ad you were shown.
An ad network counts that an ad was shown, using a limited summary report instead of a per person log.
A payment or login widget is shown in a frame that the host page cannot peek inside.
A publisher runs an ad slot on an article page without ever learning your ad profile.
A retailer retargets you with a product you viewed, without the news site you are reading ever seeing it.
A browser game shows rewarded video ads in a sealed frame so the ad cannot read the game page.

technical_bounds: No postMessage or storage sharing with the embedder; no access to the DOM from the parent
Fixed size rules for opaque URLs (no custom size) when used with auctions
Privacy Sandbox APIs were deprecated by Google in 2025; the feature remains in Chrome but ecosystem use is shrinking (verify current status)
Supported only in Chromium

abuse: Opaque ads that hide content from site owners

history.change: Fenced frames ship with Privacy Sandbox
Google announces sunset of Privacy Sandbox ad APIs

access.persistence: While the frame lives
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Needs opt-in headers (Supports-Loading-Mode: fenced-frame)
steps: Browser loads from URN or opaque URL
Frame cannot read parent, parent cannot read frame

capabilities.name: Focus and window raise
capabilities.plain: Can move focus between elements; cannot pull the window to the front or steal focus from other apps.
capabilities.meaning: A page can focus its own elements, but browsers stop it from grabbing focus from the address bar, another tab or another app, which blocks keystroke capture and pop-over scams.

limits.headline: Can move the cursor between boxes on its page, but can't pull its window forward
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you use the page, or when it finishes loading.
can: Move the typing cursor to a form box on its own page
Bring its own tab back into focus after you click on it
Highlight a button or field after you finish a step
cannot: Pull its browser window above your other apps
Steal typing from another app or another site
Jump to the front when you are in a different tab
Force a tab to open in front of the one you are in

story.what_it_is: A page can move the typing cursor between its own fields but cannot yank your whole window forward.
story.for_you: A search box can be ready to type the moment a page opens. A site cannot pull itself in front of the game or document you are using in another app.
story.for_makers: Makers use autofocus to save you a click on login and search forms. Browsers block pushing the window to the front to prevent pop under annoyances.

use_cases.example: A store's search bar is ready for typing the moment the page loads.
A browser game grabs keyboard focus on load so arrow keys work without a click.
A chat app puts the cursor in the message box after you open a conversation.
Old pop under ad tricks tried to pull a window forward, which browsers now block.
A dialog moves focus into itself and back out so keyboard and screen reader users do not get lost.
A login page puts the cursor straight into the username field.

technical_bounds: window.focus() is a no-op in modern browsers unless the person triggered it (Chrome, Safari) or dom.disable_window_flip=true (Firefox default)
Background tabs cannot raise themselves; notification clicks can focus the client via clients.focus (needs a click)
Cross-origin iframe focus() without user activation is blocked (Chrome 64)
Cannot read keystrokes outside the document or in the browser UI
autofocus on a page that is not visible does nothing

history.change: Cross-origin iframes need user activation to move focus

access.persistence: None
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframes cannot call focus() on parent or take focus without activation (Chrome 64)
steps: Browser moves focus only inside the page or when the window is already active

capabilities.name: Fullscreen
capabilities.plain: Takes over the whole screen for a page element after a click.
capabilities.meaning: A site can hide the browser UI, which helps video and games but also lets a malicious page draw a fake desktop or browser bar. Esc always exits.

limits.headline: Can make a video or page area fill your screen, after you tap
limits.user_action: You tap a Full screen button, or press a key like F on a video.
can: Fill the screen with a video, a game or a photo after a tap or key press
Hide the browser's toolbars while it is on
Stay full screen until you press Esc or swipe out
cannot: Go full screen without a tap, click or key press
Block the Esc key or the swipe that gets you out
Take over the whole iPhone screen for anything other than video
Hide that you are in full screen; browsers show a short banner
limits.differs: iPhone Safari is limited: video can go full screen, but most other page elements cannot. Android Chrome and desktop browsers allow it for any element.

story.what_it_is: After you click, a site can make part of the page fill your whole screen.

marketing.name: Fullscreen API
marketing.pitch: MDN says the API lets a site present an element, like a video or game, filling the whole screen.

story.for_you: You tap a full screen button on a video or game. The page fills your display and a small note tells you how to leave with Escape.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for immersion: video, games and slides. The click rule exists so a site cannot suddenly cover your screen with a fake desktop.

use_cases.example: You hit full screen on a movie and the player hides all the browser controls.
Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW in the browser go full screen so it feels like a console.
A presenter shows slides full screen in a web deck.
A live sports stream fills your screen for the match.
A phishing page fakes a full screen browser window to steal passwords, which is why browsers show a warning.
A student opens a full screen exam page that locks out distractions.

technical_bounds: Needs transient user activation; promise rejects with TypeError otherwise
Esc (or system gesture) always exits; with Keyboard Lock the person must hold Esc for about 2 s
Browser shows an exit notice for a few seconds; Safari desktop limits some keys in fullscreen
iPhone Safari supports only video fullscreen through the native player (requestFullscreen on elements is iPad only)
Cannot enter fullscreen without a gesture even when previously allowed; the F11 user fullscreen is separate
Password and sensitive prompts from the OS or browser still render above

abuse: Fake OS or browser UI (fullscreen spoofing)

history.change: Unprefixed requestFullscreen that returns a promise
Standard Fullscreen API on iPad (iPhone still video only)

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Ends on Esc, navigation or exitFullscreen(); no stored state
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframe needs allow="fullscreen" (Permissions Policy fullscreen defaults to self)
steps: Page calls requestFullscreen within about 5 s
Browser shows Press Esc to exit message

capabilities.name: Push history entries (back button limits)
capabilities.plain: Adds fake history entries so Back does less than expected; browsers skip entries made without a click.
capabilities.meaning: A site can change the address bar and history without loading a page. Misused, it traps the back button and keeps the person on the site, so browsers now skip entries added with no user interaction.

limits.headline: Can add extra Back button steps, but browsers skip steps made without a tap
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you move around the page, or after your first tap.
can: Change the address bar to a new page address without a full reload
Add steps so Back goes to a screen inside the app
Keep the Back button working in apps that load pages without reloading
cannot: Trap you for good on a page, because browsers skip steps made without a click or tap
Change the address to a different website
Hide where you actually are from the browser
Block you from leaving through the address bar or a bookmark

story.what_it_is: A site can add steps to your Back button list, and sometimes abuse it.

marketing.name: History API
marketing.pitch: MDN says pushState lets a page change the address bar and history without reloading.

story.for_you: When you move around a single page app, the address changes and Back works as you would expect. On bad sites, Back may seem broken because the page piled up extra entries.
story.for_makers: Single page apps use it to give each view its own link without reloading. Shady sites use it to trap people, so browsers now skip entries made without a click.

use_cases.example: Scrolling a feed and tapping a post gives a new address, so Back returns you to the feed.
A product filter updates the URL so you can share the filtered list.
Opening a document in a web app gives it its own link without a full page load.
Some ad pages stuff the Back list so that pressing Back leads to another ad page.
A streaming site opens a title in a panel and still lets Back close it.
Analytics tools watch history changes to count a new page view in single page apps.

technical_bounds: URL must be same origin as the document (SecurityError otherwise); no cross-origin path spoofing
Chrome 75 history manipulation intervention: entries added by pages that had no user interaction are skipped by Back and the long-press history menu
State object serialized size limit about 16 MiB in Firefox (browser.history.maxStateObjectSize 16 MiB); Chrome has no fixed limit but is IPC bound
Rate limits: Safari throws SecurityError after about 100 calls in 30 s; Firefox after about 200 calls in 10 s; Chrome throttles flood of navigations
Page cannot read other sites' history entries or the length beyond history.length (capped at 50 in Chrome, 50 to 1000 depending on browser)

history.change: History manipulation intervention: skip entries without user activation
Navigation API ships with entries() same-origin only
Chrome documents back-button hijacking as a spam behavior in Search and tightens intervention coverage (verify current status)

access.persistence: Entries live in the tab session history
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-origin URLs only; cross-origin frames affect the joint session history of the tab
steps: Call pushState with a same-origin URL
Back button or Navigation API fires popstate

capabilities.name: Navigate or redirect the tab
capabilities.plain: Sends the current tab to a different page by script, meta refresh or server redirect.
capabilities.meaning: A site can move the person to another URL at any time, including after they click something. Cross-origin iframes get tighter limits, which is why ad frames cannot hijack the whole tab.

limits.headline: Can send your current tab to another page by itself
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens on load, after a timer, or when you submit a form.
can: Send you to a new page after a login, a payment or a link
Move you from an old address to a new one
Open a different page in the same tab through a redirect
cannot: Send you away from a page you never opened, such as a page inside someone else's frame, in most browsers
Skip the browser's warning for a risky site
Stop you using Back; the earlier page stays in history
limits.reach_label: The tab it is running in
limits.differs: Chrome, Safari and Firefox all stop most hidden redirects from embedded frames, but how strict they are differs.

story.what_it_is: A page can send your tab to a different address by script, redirect or timer.
story.for_you: Most of the time you click a link and arrive. Sometimes you land on a different page than you clicked, for example after a login or a shortened link.
story.for_makers: Redirects are the plumbing of the web: login flows, short links, regional sites. They also power click tracking, because the hop through an ad server lets it count the click.

use_cases.example: A tap on an ad goes through a tracking server that counts the click, then forwards you to the advertiser.
You are sent to your bank, then to an identity page, then back with a signed in session.
A phishing mail link bounces you through several sites to hide the real destination.
A short link from a message expands into a long product URL with a discount code.
A browser game portal redirects you to the game's own site on a different domain.
A booking site sends you to a payment partner and then back to confirm your trip.

technical_bounds: Same-frame navigation needs no activation or prompt
Cross-origin iframe navigating the top frame is blocked without user activation (Chrome 64 framebusting intervention; sandboxed frames need allow-top-navigation*)
Navigating to data: or blob: URLs in the top frame by script is blocked in Chrome 60 and Firefox 59 for data:
Browsers cap redirect chains (Chrome and Firefox stop after 20 redirects)
Navigations flooded in a loop are throttled (Chrome IPC flooding protection, Safari 100 per 30 s)

abuse: Redirect chains used for bounce tracking

history.change: Cross-origin iframe redirects of the top frame need user activation
Block renderer-initiated top-level navigation to data: URLs

refs.label: Chrome: Prevent unwanted redirects from iframes

platform.api: location.href / assign() / replace(); <meta http-equiv=refresh>; HTTP 301/302/303/307/308; top.location from an iframe

access.persistence: One-shot; no stored state
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframe may navigate top only with user activation (sandbox allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation) or allow-top-navigation
steps: Script runs location.assign or sets location.href
beforeunload may ask the person to stay

capabilities.name: Navigation API
capabilities.plain: Gives a single place to listen to and control same-document navigations.
capabilities.meaning: A single page app can intercept link clicks and back or forward, and list its own history entries. It sees only same-origin entries, so it cannot read browsing history.

limits.headline: Can watch and control page changes inside the app, such as when you press Back
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you click links, press Back, or move around the app.
can: Notice when you click a link or press Back inside the site
Update the page without a full reload
Hold up a page change until a save finishes
cannot: Watch what you do on other sites or in other tabs
Block you from leaving the site
Change the address to another site's address
See where you came from outside its own pages

story.what_it_is: A modern way for a page to manage its own links and Back button handling.

marketing.name: Navigation API
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say the API modernizes single page app routing with one clear set of tools.

story.for_you: You never see it. When it works, apps feel snappier and Back and Forward behave more predictably inside big web apps.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to build cleaner routing than the older history tricks, with animation hooks and a proper list of past entries. It is mostly a developer quality and speed win.

use_cases.example: A web mail app changes folders without reloading and keeps Back working.
A streaming site slides between pages with an animation while loading the next view.
A store keeps your scroll position when you press Back from a product.
A framework wires its router to the API so one place handles every in page link.
A measurement script catches every in page navigation without brittle hacks.
A live blog moves between match pages without breaking the real time feed.

technical_bounds: entries() lists only same-origin entries of the current tab
The same back button hijack mitigations apply (entries without user activation are skippable)
Cannot read other tabs or other origins' history
Support per MDN BCD: Chrome 102, Safari 26.2, Firefox 147

access.persistence: Entries live in the tab session
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-origin entries only

capabilities.name: Open popup or new window
capabilities.plain: Opens a new tab or popup window, but only right after a click or tap.
capabilities.meaning: A site can put another page in front of the person (ads, login flows, payment pages). Popup blockers decide whether it happens, so it is the main way a site can steer attention to a second origin.

limits.headline: Can open a new tab or window, but only right after you tap or click
limits.user_action: You tap a link, a button, or Share, Print or Open in new tab.
can: Open a new tab or small window after a tap or click
Open a sign in window for a login or a payment
Open a link in a new tab you can close
cannot: Open a window with no tap or click, which browsers block by default
Open lots of windows from one tap in most cases
Control a window that belongs to a different site
Hide the address bar of the new window in modern browsers
limits.differs: iPhone Safari is a little stricter about which taps count.

story.what_it_is: After a click, a page can open a new tab or small window.
story.for_you: You click a link and a new tab opens, or you sign in with Google and a small window appears. Without a click, the browser blocks the pop up.
story.for_makers: Makers use pop ups for sign in windows, payment confirmations and help chats. The click rule exists because pop up ads were once everywhere.

use_cases.example: Clicking 'Sign in with Google' opens a small window to approve, then closes.
A PayPal button opens a small window to confirm payment, then returns you to the shop.
A shady ad site tries to open a new tab with every click anywhere on the page.
A browser game portal opens the leaderboard in a pop up.
A streamer's chat is popped out to a separate window so it can sit on a second monitor.
A bank opens a secure help chat in a small window.

technical_bounds: Blocked without transient user activation (Chrome, Safari, Firefox all block popups outside input handlers)
Transient activation lasts about 5 s in Chrome and Firefox (dom.user_activation.transient.timeout = 5000 ms); Safari uses a much shorter window (about 1 s)
window.open consumes the activation in Chrome and Safari, so a second popup in the same click is blocked
Firefox allows up to dom.popup_maximum (default 20) popups from one event
target=_blank and window.open imply noopener for links (Chrome 88, Firefox 79, Safari 12.1)
Popup features width and height are clamped to a minimum of 100 CSS px; position cannot be placed off screen

abuse: Phishing windows that mimic browser chrome

history.change: Popups opened from user clicks only; blocker icon in the address bar
Popups in cross-origin iframes limited; abusive redirect and popup interventions
Anchors with target=_blank get implicit rel=noopener
popup=true feature and window.open consumes transient activation across browsers (HTML spec)

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Per window; users can allow pop-ups per site (Chrome Pop-ups and redirects setting, Firefox exceptions, Safari per-site setting)
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Needs sandbox allow-popups (and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox for unsandboxed children)
steps: Handler calls window.open within about 5 s of the click
Browser opens window or shows blocked-popup icon

capabilities.name: Background tab timer throttling
capabilities.plain: Hidden tabs get slower timers: 1 per second, then 1 per minute after 5 minutes in Chrome.
capabilities.meaning: Tells the site whether the tab is visible and caps how much it can do while hidden. Useful for battery, but sites also detect tab switches via visibilitychange.

limits.headline: Can't keep its timers running fast once you switch to another tab
limits.user_action: You switch to another tab or app and leave the page.
can: Run its code once a second while the tab is hidden
Keep playing sound, if the page plays audio
Slow down by itself to save battery
cannot: Keep fast timers in a hidden tab; they drop to once a second, then once a minute after 5 minutes in Chrome
Stay running as normal after you lock your phone
Turn off the browser's own power saving limit
Do heavy work in the background without a background task such as a worker or a service worker

story.what_it_is: When a tab is hidden, the browser slows its clocks to save battery.

marketing.name: Timer throttling in Chrome 88
marketing.pitch: Chrome explains that background tabs get less frequent timers, to save power and CPU.

story.for_you: You switch away from a tab and your laptop fan stays quiet. The cost is that some live things, like a countdown or a game, may lag or stall until you return.
story.for_makers: Makers must design around it: pause animations, use server time, and keep calls and live connections alive for real time apps. Browsers use it to keep ads and trackers from burning battery.

use_cases.example: An idle game or a browser multiplayer game must handle the tab being frozen, or it drops you from the match.
A live auction or sports score page catches up with the server when you return to its tab.
A video call tab keeps audio running even when hidden, because audio is allowed to play.
Ad measurement counts a view only when the tab is visible, so hidden tabs do not inflate numbers.
A web chat app uses a push connection so it notifies you even when throttled.
Time on page tools pause counting when the tab is hidden.

technical_bounds: Chrome 57: budget based throttling; hidden timers wake about once per second
Chrome 88 intensive throttling: after 5 min hidden, timer chains of 5 or more run once per minute (page silent 30 s, not using WebRTC or audio)
Exempt: audible tabs, active WebRTC data channels or media streams, pages with Web Locks or IndexedDB transactions in flight
requestAnimationFrame pauses completely in hidden tabs; Safari throttles to 1 s then suspends; Firefox clamps to 1 s (and 10 s in some setups)
Memory Saver (Chrome 108+) can discard inactive tabs; wasDiscarded reveals prior discard

history.change: Intensive wake up throttling after 5 minutes hidden
Page Lifecycle API with freeze and resume

platform.api: document.visibilityState, visibilitychange; setTimeout/setInterval; Page Lifecycle freeze/resume

access.persistence: While hidden
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Applies per page, including iframes
steps: Chrome aligns timers to 1 s; after 5 min with chained timers it runs them once per minute
Page can be frozen then discarded

capabilities.name: Popover and modal dialog
capabilities.plain: Shows overlays on top of everything on the page using the top layer.
capabilities.meaning: A site can draw modal dialogs and popovers above all other content, including iframes. They are page content, not browser UI, so well made fakes can mimic prompts.

limits.headline: Can show a box over everything else on the page
limits.user_action: Nothing for most boxes. It happens when you tap a menu, a help bubble or Open details.
can: Show a menu, tooltip or confirm box on top of the page
Dim and lock the page behind a modal box until you close it
Close the box when you press Esc or tap outside
cannot: Cover things outside its own page, like the address bar or other tabs
Stop you leaving the tab or closing the browser
Show over another app on your phone or computer

story.what_it_is: A page can put a box on top of everything, using built in browser tools.

marketing.name: Popover API
marketing.pitch: Chrome's blog says the Popover API lets developers show floating content above the rest of the page with little code.

story.for_you: Menus, tooltips and 'accept cookies' boxes sit neatly on top of the page, and keyboard and screen readers handle them better than home made versions.
story.for_makers: Makers replace fragile custom code with built in pieces. It means fewer bugs, better accessibility and lighter pages, and it standardizes how consent banners and menus work.

use_cases.example: A product page opens a size chart as a modal that dims the page behind it.
A cookie consent banner is drawn on top of the whole page by the site.
A modal traps keyboard focus so someone using a screen reader cannot tab behind it.
A browser game shows a pause menu on top of the playing field.
A dropdown menu in a web app pops open above the rest of the page.
A photo viewer opens a lightbox over a feed.

technical_bounds: No activation required to show a dialog or popover (activation required for fullscreen only)
Cannot draw outside the viewport or over the address bar and permission bubbles
popover=auto uses light dismiss; popover=manual does not
Support: dialog Chrome 37, Safari 15.4, Firefox 98; popover Chrome 114, Safari 17, Firefox 125

abuse: Fake browser permission dialogs drawn inside the page

access.persistence: While open
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Top layer belongs to each document; cannot cover browser UI

capabilities.name: Open the print dialog
capabilities.plain: Opens the system print dialog for the page, no click required in most browsers.
capabilities.meaning: A site can ask to print itself or a hidden frame. It cannot choose a printer or print silently, and it cannot read what the person does in the dialog.

limits.headline: Can open your print window, without a click in most browsers
limits.user_action: Nothing in most cases. It happens when the page runs a print command, or you tap Print.
can: Open the print dialog for the current page
Format the page for print with its own print styles
Let you save the page as a PDF from the print window
cannot: Print without you pressing Print in the dialog
Pick a printer or change the settings for you
See what printer you use or what your printer is called
Print in the background after you leave the page

story.what_it_is: A page can open your print window, usually without asking.
story.for_you: A receipt or ticket page may open the print box by itself. You can always cancel it. Nothing prints until you confirm.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for receipts, tickets and reports, so you get a clean paper version in one step. Print style sheets also let one page look right on screen and on paper.

use_cases.example: After booking, a boarding pass page opens the print box so you can print it.
A statement page offers a print button with a layout cleaned for paper.
An order confirmation has a Print receipt button.
A school portal prints a certificate or a worksheet.
An online document tool prints a neat version without the toolbars.
A warehouse tool prints shipping labels as soon as an order is packed.

technical_bounds: Blocks the page until the dialog is dismissed in most browsers
Cannot print silently, choose the printer, or read the print result (no kiosk printing without enterprise policy)
Chrome ignores print() in sandboxed iframes lacking allow-modals
Repeated print() calls are not rate limited in the spec; Chrome limits when the tab is in the background
Page cannot read the printed output or the printer list

history.change: Print from sandboxed iframes requires allow-modals

access.persistence: One-shot
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Sandboxed frames need allow-modals; cross-origin frames print only their own content
steps: afterprint fires when the dialog closes

capabilities.name: Task scheduling (postTask, yield)
capabilities.plain: Lets a page prioritize its own tasks and yield to input so it stays responsive.
capabilities.meaning: A site can order its work and split long tasks. It cannot run when the tab is hidden any faster; it only improves smoothness inside the page.

limits.headline: Can sort its own tasks so the page stays quick when you tap
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens while the page runs and you scroll or tap.
can: Run important page tasks before less important ones
Pause its own long work so taps and scrolls feel smooth
Cancel or move its own queued tasks
cannot: Change what other tabs or other sites do
Speed up the device itself
Skip the browser's own power saving rules
Work in Safari or on iPhone, where it is not offered yet
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge and Firefox support it. Safari, including on iPhone, does not yet.

story.what_it_is: A page can rank its own jobs so it stays responsive when you tap.

marketing.name: Optimize long tasks
marketing.pitch: Chrome's web.dev guide teaches splitting work and yielding so pages respond quickly to taps and keys.

story.for_you: You never see it. A page that uses it responds faster when you tap a button while it is still loading something else.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to meet speed scores that affect search ranking and sales. Giving the browser room to handle taps first makes heavy pages feel quick.

use_cases.example: A busy product page loads reviews in the background so the Add to cart button answers right away.
A browser game keeps frames steady by deferring low priority work, like loading far away level pieces.
A big web spreadsheet recalculates in small chunks so typing is not delayed.
Measurement scripts are queued at low priority so they do not slow the page.
Ads load at a lower priority than the article text.
A feed renders posts slice by slice as you scroll.

technical_bounds: Priorities: user-blocking, user-visible, background
Does not bypass background tab throttling
Support per MDN BCD: Chrome 94 (postTask) and 129 (yield), Firefox 142, no Safari support

access.persistence: None
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag
steps: Browser runs it after higher priority work

capabilities.name: Beacons and keepalive requests
capabilities.plain: Sends data after the person leaves or closes the page, with no prompt.
capabilities.meaning: A site can finish sending analytics even as the tab closes. It is the standard way for page leave metrics, and the reason tab closing does not stop data from being sent.

limits.headline: Can send data to a server as you leave or close the page
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you close the tab, switch away or tap a link.
can: Send a small report to its server when you leave
Save your last scroll spot, a score or a form draft to the server
Finish a request even as the page shuts
cannot: Send large amounts of data; browsers cap each beacon at about 64 KB
Wait for or use an answer from the server
Keep going after the browser kills the page

story.what_it_is: A page can send a last message to its server as you leave, and you will not notice.

marketing.name: Navigator.sendBeacon()
marketing.pitch: MDN describes it as a way to send small amounts of data to a server reliably when a page closes.

story.for_you: You never see it. When you close a tab, a quiet message may still go out saying how long you stayed, how far you scrolled or whether a video finished.
story.for_makers: It is the standard way to record the end of a visit for analytics, ads and error reports. It matters because regular requests are cancelled when the page closes and those last numbers would be lost.

use_cases.example: Google Analytics sends the final page timing as you close the tab.
An ad network logs that you viewed an ad for 12 seconds before leaving.
A streaming player reports your last watched second so playback resumes on another device.
An error tool sends crash details even if the page is closing.
A browser game saves your score as you close the tab.
A fraud tool records behaviour signals up to the very last moment of a login page visit.

technical_bounds: Keepalive in-flight body limit about 64 KiB per origin in Chrome (shared with sendBeacon)
Response cannot be read
Use visibilitychange or pagehide, not unload (BFCache)
fetchLater() ships in Chrome and Edge 135 (not Firefox or Safari) and defers a request until the page is gone; documented quota about 64 KiB per origin and 512 KiB per document

access.persistence: One request, queued by the browser
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag
steps: Call sendBeacon in pagehide or visibilitychange

capabilities.name: Service Worker offline caching
capabilities.plain: Installs a script that caches pages and answers requests when offline.
capabilities.meaning: A site can keep running its own code between visits and serve content from a local cache. Safari deletes script-written storage after 7 days without interaction; Chrome keeps it until cleared.

limits.headline: Can save pages on your device so the site works offline
limits.user_action: You open the site once. It installs by itself, with no pop up.
can: Save pages, images and files on your device for later
Show saved pages when you have no signal
Answer or change requests the site makes, even when you are offline
cannot: Work on a site that has not been opened over a secure connection (HTTPS)
Use unlimited storage; browsers set a limit and may clear it
Stay saved forever; Safari on iPhone can clear it after 7 days of no use
Reach other sites' saved files
limits.reach_label: Stays on your device between visits
limits.differs: Safari on iPhone can clear saved data after about 7 days without a visit, unless the site is added to your Home Screen.

story.what_it_is: A site can install a helper that stores pages and works when you are offline.

marketing.name: Service workers
marketing.pitch: web.dev teaches service workers as the base of installable, offline capable web apps.

story.for_you: A site opens instantly the second time and may even work on a plane. You never approve it, and it lives on after you close the tab.
story.for_makers: Makers get offline use, quick starts and push messages, which lifts return visits. It also lets them update an app silently in the background.

use_cases.example: A music or podcast web app plays saved episodes with no signal.
A flight status or map site loads from its saved copy in an airport with weak wifi.
A lite social site opens in a flash on a slow phone.
A browser game stores its art and levels so it starts fast and plays offline.
A store saves its catalog shell so browsing is fast on a bad connection.
A malicious site may keep a helper installed to serve ads or show alerts later, which is why you can clear site data.

technical_bounds: HTTPS or localhost only
Idle service workers terminate after about 30 s; a single event can run up to about 5 minutes in Chrome
Browser checks for a new worker script at most every 24 h (byte compare) and on navigation
Safari (ITP) caps script-writable storage including service worker registrations and Cache API at 7 days of no user interaction (not for Home Screen web apps)
Cache API quota shared with origin quota (Chrome up to 60% of disk per origin; Firefox about 10% of disk, up to 10 GiB per group)
Cannot run while the browser is closed except via push or background sync (permission and platform needed)

abuse: Persistent foothold for tracking and malware

history.change: ITP caps script-writable storage including SW at 7 days

access.persistence: Persists until unregistered or storage cleared; Safari ITP may delete after 7 days of no interaction
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same origin only; scope limited to script path unless Service-Worker-Allowed header is set
steps: fetch events return cached or network responses

capabilities.name: Speculation Rules (prefetch and prerender)
capabilities.plain: A page can tell the browser to load and render the next page in the background.
capabilities.meaning: A site can preload other URLs the person may visit. Prerendered pages run scripts before the person arrives, so analytics and counters may fire on a visit that never happens.

limits.headline: Can tell your browser to load the likely next page before you tap
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you hover over or get close to a link.
can: Load the next page in the background before you tap it
Show the next page right away when you do tap
Pick pages to preload on its own site
cannot: Preload pages when your browser has data saver or low power on
Run the other page's sign in or purchase actions
Preload pages from other sites with your logged in details
Work in Firefox
limits.reach_label: Only its own likely next pages
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge and Safari support it. Firefox does not yet.

story.what_it_is: A page can tell the browser to load the next page before you click it.

marketing.name: Prerender pages in Chrome
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say prerendering the likely next page can make navigation feel instant.

story.for_you: The next page appears almost instantly when you click. What you do not see is that your browser may have loaded it for you earlier, even if you never opened it.
story.for_makers: Makers bet on where you will click next and load it early to boost speed, which lifts search ranking and sales. The cost is extra data use and the site may count visits you never made.

use_cases.example: On a store listing, the top product page is loaded in the background so tapping it feels instant.
A news site prerenders the next top story from the home page.
A streaming service prefetches the title page of a show you are hovering over.
Analytics must avoid counting prerendered pages that the person never actually viewed.
An ad system waits to count an impression until a prerendered page is really shown.
A booking site prerenders the next step of search results.

technical_bounds: Chrome limits: eagerness immediate or eager up to 50 prefetches and 10 prerenders; moderate or conservative up to 2 (FIFO)
Disabled when Data Saver or Energy Saver is on, when Preload pages is off, or memory is low
Prerendered pages defer permission prompts, notifications, geolocation and other sensitive APIs until activation
Cross-origin prerender is not allowed; same-site cross-origin prefetch needs opt in
Support per MDN BCD: Chrome and Edge 109, Safari 27.3; Firefox has not shipped it

abuse: Loading pages to disclose IP or cookies before click

history.change: Prefetch and prerender via speculation rules

access.persistence: While the page is open; discarded when not used
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-site prerender by default; cross-origin prefetch needs opt-in
steps: Browser fetches or prerenders per eagerness

capabilities.name: Speech synthesis (text to speech)
capabilities.plain: Speaks text aloud with the device's voices; needs a prior interaction.
capabilities.meaning: A site can read text out loud with built-in voices. The voice list differs by device, so it also hints at the OS, language packs and installed software.

limits.headline: Can speak text out loud, after you have tapped on the page
limits.user_action: You tap Listen or Play aloud, or tap the page before it speaks.
can: Speak text out loud using voices on your device
Pause, resume or stop the voice
Pick a voice from the ones on your device
cannot: Speak the moment a page loads, before you have tapped or clicked
Record you or hear what you say
Use voices you do not have on your device

story.what_it_is: A page can read text out loud with your device's voices.

marketing.name: Web Speech API
marketing.pitch: MDN says speech synthesis lets pages read text aloud with the voices on your device.

story.for_you: You tap a Listen button and a voice reads an article or a language lesson. The browser blocks a page from talking before you have touched it.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for accessibility, language apps and hands free reading. It costs them nothing because the device does the voice work.

use_cases.example: A language app reads a Spanish word aloud so you can hear the accent.
A news site offers a Listen to this article button.
A screen reading tool speaks page text for people with low vision or dyslexia.
A browser game has a robot narrator reading dialog out loud.
A web note app reads your note back to you while you cook.
A children's reading site speaks each word as the child taps it.

risks: Voice list can identify a device

technical_bounds: Chrome 71 requires user activation on the page before speak() produces sound
Utterance rate 0.1 to 10, pitch 0 to 2, volume 0 to 1
Network voices in Chrome (Google voices) historically stop after about 15 s of speech (known issue)
Cannot record the output or pick voices not installed
Voice list and default voice leak OS and language (fingerprint)

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Voices list fixed per OS; queue lasts for the page
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframes need allow="autoplay"-like activation in that frame

capabilities.name: Change tab title and icon
capabilities.plain: Changes the tab title and icon at any time, including while the tab is in the background.
capabilities.meaning: A site can animate the title, add unread counts, or swap the favicon. It is a no-prompt way to draw attention from a hidden tab; scammers also use it to mimic other sites.

limits.headline: Can change its tab name and small icon at any time
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you use the page, even when the tab is hidden.
can: Change the tab name, such as to show a new message count
Swap the small icon in the tab
Change them even when you are in another tab
cannot: Change the title or icon of other sites or tabs
Change what is in your bookmarks without you saving it
Hide the real site address in the address bar

story.what_it_is: A page can change its tab name, icon and badge, even when you are looking elsewhere.

marketing.name: Badging API
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say the badging API lets an installed web app show a number on its icon.

story.for_you: Your tab shows '(3) Inbox' or blinks a dot when something new arrives. You feel pulled back to check it, even though you never asked for alerts.
story.for_makers: Makers use it as a free attention nudge: unread counts, call status, game turns. It works without any permission, so it reaches everyone.

use_cases.example: Your mail tab shows an unread count and flashes when a new email arrives.
A live auction tab shows 'Outbid!' in its title so you notice.
A browser strategy game flashes 'Your turn' in the tab title.
A video call shows who is speaking in the tab icon.
A shady site changes its title and icon to look like a bank or a warning.
A project tool shows a spinner icon while it saves.

technical_bounds: No limit on title length in the DOM; tab strips truncate to about the first 20 to 40 characters
Favicon cache may delay updates (Chrome, Safari cache aggressively)
Badging API works only for installed apps in Chrome and Safari 17 Home Screen web apps; no prompt in installed apps for the numeric badge but notifications permission is needed on iOS
Page cannot flash the taskbar or play a system sound without media or notification permission

abuse: Tab title swap after the person leaves (tabnabbing)

history.change: Badging API for installed PWAs on desktop

access.persistence: Until navigation
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Frames cannot change the top document title
steps: Script sets document.title or the icon href
App badge needs an installed PWA (Chrome desktop 81)

capabilities.name: Scroll to text fragment
capabilities.plain: Highlights and scrolls to quoted text in a page when a link includes #:~:text=.
capabilities.meaning: A link can point at one sentence on any page. The browser, not the page, does the highlighting, and the page cannot see the fragment, so it cannot learn what the visitor was searching for.

limits.headline: Can scroll to and highlight text on a page when you open a special link
limits.user_action: You tap a link that ends with a text highlight, like a link shared from search results.
can: Jump to quoted text on the page and highlight it
Open from a link that someone shared with you
Show a short highlight in yellow
cannot: Let the page's own code see which text was highlighted
Highlight text that is not on the page
Highlight text inside embedded frames in most cases
Run without you opening that link

story.what_it_is: A link can highlight and scroll to exact words on a page.

marketing.name: Text fragments
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say you can link right to a specific passage of a page.

story.for_you: You tap a link and the page jumps to a highlighted sentence. Search results use it so you land on the answer, not the top of the page.
story.for_makers: Makers and search engines use it to send people to the exact passage. Google search snippets use it and some sharing tools make quote links with it.

use_cases.example: A search result links to the exact sentence that answers your question.
A reader copies a link to a quote from an article and sends it to a friend.
A teacher links students to the exact definition inside a long page.
A research tool saves quotes as links back to the highlighted text.
A site may use it to find out whether specific words exist on a page.
A docs site links straight to the line about a function.

technical_bounds: Needs user activation or browser-initiated navigation (search results, address bar)
Page script cannot read the directive (stripped from location.hash and document.fragmentDirective is empty)
Matches visible text only, word boundary aware, first match wins
Cross-origin initiated navigations need noopener; not applied in iframes
Can be disabled by Document-Policy: force-load-at-top

abuse: Probing page contents with crafted links (mitigated by activation, no readable fragment)

access.persistence: One-shot per navigation
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Only full navigations in top-level browsing contexts
steps: Person opens a link with a text directive
Browser finds the first match and scrolls
Highlight is drawn by the browser

capabilities.name: Vibrate the device
capabilities.plain: Triggers the phone's vibration motor in short pulses.
capabilities.meaning: A site can buzz the device for feedback or alerts. It is Android only, needs a tap first, and cannot run from hidden frames or background tabs.

limits.headline: Can buzz the phone in short pulses, after you have tapped the page
limits.user_action: You tap a button, win a game, or touch the page before it buzzes.
can: Buzz your Android phone in a pattern after a tap
Stop a buzz it started
Give touch feedback in games and timers
cannot: Buzz without any earlier tap on the page
Buzz on iPhone, because Safari does not offer it
Buzz in current Firefox, which no longer offers it
limits.differs: Android Chrome and Edge allow it. iPhone Safari does not.

story.what_it_is: A site can make your phone buzz in short bursts after you tap.

marketing.name: Vibration API
marketing.pitch: MDN says the Vibration API lets a page buzz the phone for feedback.

story.for_you: You tap a button in a web game or app and feel a short buzz. Safari on iPhone does not allow it, so you only feel it on some phones.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for touch feedback that makes a web app feel like a real app. It is cheap and needs no permission, only a recent tap.

use_cases.example: A browser racing or shooter game buzzes when you crash or get hit.
A web chat app buzzes your phone for a new message when it is open.
A checkout page buzzes once when the payment goes through.
A workout timer buzzes at the end of each set.
A web app buzzes to confirm a tap for people who cannot see well.
An annoying ad may try to buzz the phone to get attention, which Chrome blocks without a tap.

technical_bounds: Needs sticky user activation in the frame (Chrome 60); no prompt
Pattern limited to 99 entries and 10 s per entry in Chrome (about); longer values truncated
Not available in Safari or any iOS browser; Firefox desktop removed it in 129
Stops when the tab is hidden or screen locks
Hardware intensity cannot be set; only on and off durations

history.change: Cross-origin iframe vibrate needs activation in that frame
Vibration API removed from desktop Firefox

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: One-shot pattern; cancelled by vibrate(0) or tab hide
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Blocked in cross-origin iframes without prior activation in that frame (Firefox 72, Chrome 77)
steps: Person taps in the page (sticky activation in the frame)

capabilities.name: View Transitions
capabilities.plain: Animates between page states, including across same-origin navigations.
capabilities.meaning: A site can capture a screenshot of the old and new state and morph between them. Cross-document transitions work only within one origin, so it cannot reveal another site's pixels.

limits.headline: Can animate smoothly between two page screens on its own site
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you tap a link or the page updates.
can: Fade or slide between two screens
Animate a picture moving from a list to a detail page
Keep a smooth look when you move between pages on the same site
cannot: Animate between two different sites
See what is on the other page before it loads

story.what_it_is: A page can animate smoothly from one screen to the next.

marketing.name: View Transition API
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say it creates smooth animated transitions between views, even across pages.

story.for_you: Moving between pages feels like moving inside a phone app: a picture grows into a detail view and nothing flashes white.
story.for_makers: Makers get app like polish with a few lines of code, which helps keep people engaged and makes a site feel premium.

use_cases.example: A product photo grows from a grid thumbnail into the detail page.
A movie poster expands into the title page.
A browser game cross fades between menus and levels.
A story card slides open into the full article.
A portfolio site glides between project pages.
A web dashboard animates panels as you switch tabs.

technical_bounds: Cross-document transitions are same-origin only (Chrome 126, Safari 18.2)
Callback timeout about 4 s before the transition is skipped (Chrome)
Does not read or leak cross-origin pixels; snapshots exclude cross-origin iframes content
Support: same-document Chrome 111, Safari 18, Firefox 144

access.persistence: While animating
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-origin cross-document only

capabilities.name: Web Audio playback
capabilities.plain: Plays generated sound; the audio context stays silent until the person has interacted.
capabilities.meaning: A site can synthesize and mix sound at sample precision (games, music tools). Autoplay rules keep it quiet until a click, but once resumed it can run for as long as the tab lives.

limits.headline: Can play and mix sound inside the page, after you have tapped
limits.user_action: You tap Play, Start or anything on the page before sound begins.
can: Play sounds, music or game effects that it makes or loads
Mix and change sounds, such as echo and volume
Keep sound going while the tab is open
cannot: Make sound before you have tapped, clicked or pressed a key
Listen through your microphone; that needs a separate permission
Play over a tab you muted yourself
Change your device volume

story.what_it_is: A page can make sound, but stays silent until you click or tap.

marketing.name: Autoplay policy in Chrome
marketing.pitch: Chrome explains that sound only plays after you interact with the page.

story.for_you: A game or music tool starts making sound only after your first tap. You are never surprised by blaring audio from a new tab.
story.for_makers: Makers get full control over sound: effects, synths and mixing. The gesture rule is how browsers keep ads from shouting at you.

use_cases.example: A browser game plays footsteps, music and echo effects, all built from code.
A web music maker lets you play synths and drums in the browser.
A video call tool adds noise cancelling to your voice.
A learning site shows how a sound wave works and plays it.
Audio processing can reveal small differences between devices and is used in fingerprinting.
An ad network tries to autoplay a video ad with sound, blocked until you tap.
