technical_bounds: AudioContext starts suspended until user activation on the page (Chrome 71, Firefox 66, Safari since webkitAudioContext)
Chrome limits about 6 simultaneously active AudioContexts per tab in older versions; Safari limits 4 on iOS (older)
Cannot choose output device without setSinkId and a permission (selectAudioOutput)
Sample rate and output latency are readable (fingerprint)
Cannot read the system volume or other apps' audio

history.change: AudioContext.setSinkId lets a page route output to a chosen device

access.prompt_ui: No prompt (needs a click, tap or keypress)
access.persistence: Context state suspended until resumed; lives with the page
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Cross-origin iframes need allow="autoplay"
steps: Audio plays through the default output

capabilities.name: Web Crypto (non-extractable keys)
capabilities.plain: Provides built-in cryptography; keys can be stored in the browser and marked non-exportable.
capabilities.meaning: A site can encrypt data, sign with keys it cannot export, and store them in IndexedDB. Non-extractable keys stop theft by script but do not stop a malicious page using them.

limits.headline: Can lock and unlock data inside the page, with keys it can't hand out
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page signs in, saves data or checks a file.
can: Create secure keys and random numbers
Scramble and unscramble data
Check that a file has not been changed
cannot: Hand out a key that was made non exportable
Reach keys saved by other sites
Work on a page that is not on a secure connection (HTTPS)
Keep its saved keys after you clear that site's data

story.what_it_is: The browser has built in locks and keys that a page can use and store safely.

marketing.name: Web Crypto API
marketing.pitch: MDN says the API gives pages tools for hashing, signing, encryption and key handling.

story.for_you: You never see it. It quietly protects logins, chats and payments, and keeps your keys in a form that scripts cannot read out.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to secure logins, sign messages and encrypt data in your browser before it leaves. Non exportable keys help stop theft even if the page is attacked.

use_cases.example: A secure chat tool encrypts messages in your browser before sending.
A bank page signs a login challenge with a key that never leaves the browser.
A password manager web app encrypts your vault locally.
A notes app does end to end encryption of your documents.
A browser game signs scores so cheaters cannot send fake ones.
Ad scripts use random numbers from the same tool to create ids.

technical_bounds: crypto.subtle only in secure contexts
Non-extractable keys cannot be exported via exportKey(), but any script on the origin can use them
getRandomValues fills at most 65536 bytes per call
Algorithms: AES-GCM and CBC and CTR, RSA-OAEP and PSS, ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521), ECDH, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, SHA-1/256/384/512; Ed25519 (Chrome 137, Safari 17, Firefox 129), X25519
No hardware-backed keys (use WebAuthn for that)

access.persistence: CryptoKey objects can be stored in IndexedDB as opaque handles
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: HTTPS only (crypto.subtle undefined on HTTP except localhost)

capabilities.name: Web Workers
capabilities.plain: Runs scripts on background threads with no prompt.
capabilities.meaning: A site can use multiple CPU cores while the tab is open. Workers cannot touch the DOM but can run timers, network and compute, which is how miners and heavy trackers hide from the UI thread.

limits.headline: Can run extra code in the background while the page is open
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads or starts a heavy job.
can: Run heavy work on a second thread so the page stays smooth
Keep a worker running while the tab is open
Run several workers at once
cannot: Change what is on the page directly
Keep running after you close the tab
Use unlimited power; browsers slow hidden tabs
Reach other sites' workers or data

story.what_it_is: A page can run extra background workers, with no prompt.

marketing.name: Web Workers API
marketing.pitch: MDN says workers let a page run scripts in background threads so the main page stays responsive.

story.for_you: You never see them. Heavy tasks like photo editing run in the background so the page does not freeze while you type.
story.for_makers: Makers use them to keep pages smooth while crunching data. Bad actors use the same trick to mine crypto in your tab without telling you.

use_cases.example: A photo editor applies filters in a worker so sliders stay smooth.
A browser game runs physics and AI on a worker so the frame rate does not drop.
A video call tool blurs your background in a worker.
A hidden crypto miner runs in a worker in a shady site tab.
A web spreadsheet recalculates in a worker so typing stays quick.
Analytics tools process events in a worker to avoid slowing the page.

technical_bounds: Firefox limits to 512 workers per domain (dom.workers.maxPerDomain); Chrome has no fixed cap but memory limited
Background tabs throttle timers in workers just like pages; intensive throttling applies
SharedWorker returned to Android Chrome at version 148 (BCD); long absent on mobile
No access to window, document or localStorage; IndexedDB, fetch, WebSockets work
Worker script must be same origin (or data via importScripts with CORS)

access.persistence: Dedicated workers end with the page; shared workers end when the last client closes
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Same-origin script only; module workers supported; blob: workers allowed

capabilities.name: WebAssembly (threads, SIMD, memory limits)
capabilities.plain: Runs compiled code at near native speed inside the page, with up to 4 GB of memory (16 GB with memory64 in Chrome).
capabilities.meaning: A site can run heavy code (games, codecs, Photoshop-class tools) with no install. The same speed makes in-browser miners and side channel timing code practical.

limits.headline: Can run fast compiled code inside the page, within memory limits
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, such as a game, editor or video tool.
can: Run apps made in languages like C++ or Rust inside the page
Use up to 4 GB of memory per page; Chrome can go to 16 GB with memory64
Use several threads at once when the site is isolated
cannot: Skip the browser's rules for web code; it runs in the same safe sandbox
Reach your files, camera or other apps on its own
Use more memory than the limit the browser sets
Run after you close the page

story.what_it_is: A page can run big, compiled programs in your browser at near desktop speed.

marketing.name: WebAssembly
marketing.pitch: The WebAssembly site pitches it as a fast, safe binary format that runs in browsers next to JavaScript.

story.for_you: You open a web app and it feels like a desktop program. Photoshop or a 3D game loads in a tab without an install.
story.for_makers: Makers can bring huge existing programs to the web without rewriting them. This is how big games, CAD and design tools reach anyone with a link.

use_cases.example: Figma runs its design engine as WebAssembly so large files stay smooth.
Unity and Unreal games run in a tab, and Doom style ports run at full speed.
A web conferencing client uses it to compress and clean video and audio.
AutoCAD and Google Earth run in a browser tab using compiled code.
Attackers can hide crypto miners or obfuscated code in compiled form, harder to inspect.
Developers run Python or full databases in the browser with no server.

technical_bounds: wasm32 memory max 65536 pages = 4 GiB per memory in Chrome and Firefox; Safari and mobile browsers often cap lower (about 1 to 2 GiB in practice)
memory64 raises the limit to 16 GiB in V8 (Chrome 133, Firefox 134); real allocations still fail when RAM is short
Threads need SharedArrayBuffer and cross-origin isolation (COOP and COEP)
SIMD: Chrome 91, Firefox 89, Safari 16.4; also tail calls (Chrome 112), GC (Chrome 119, Firefox 120, Safari 18.2)
Under a CSP without 'wasm-unsafe-eval', compile is blocked (Chrome 97)
Sandbox: no direct OS access, only imports provided by JavaScript

access.persistence: While the page lives
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag; CSP script-src needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval' to compile

capabilities.name: WebCodecs (video and audio encode and decode)
capabilities.plain: Gives direct access to the browser's video and audio codecs with no prompt.
capabilities.meaning: A site can encode or decode media frames in code, often with hardware acceleration. Great for editors, but also lets a page probe which codecs and accelerators the device has.

limits.headline: Can open and make video and sound files by itself inside the page
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page plays, edits or records media.
can: Decode video and audio frame by frame
Make new video or audio files in the page
Use your device's chip to speed up video
cannot: Turn on your camera or microphone without a permission pop up
Go past what your device's chip can handle
Work on files it was not given
Run after you close the page

story.what_it_is: A page can use your device's video and sound chips directly to pack and unpack media.

marketing.name: WebCodecs
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say WebCodecs gives low level control over video and audio encoding and decoding in the browser.

story.for_you: You never see it. Web video editors, cloud games and calls just look sharper and use less battery, because the page uses hardware built for video.
story.for_makers: Makers get fast video processing without a plugin: custom players, editing, streaming with very low delay. It turns a tab into a serious media tool.

use_cases.example: Cloud gaming in a browser decodes the game video stream frame by frame with very little delay.
A web video editor cuts, exports and previews clips using hardware encoding.
A video call app packs your camera into small frames for the network.
A live streaming tool sends your webcam to viewers at very low delay.
A camera monitoring dashboard decodes many streams at once for a security guard.
A video ad player decodes ads with exact timing, so the ad counts as viewed.

technical_bounds: isConfigSupported() reveals codec and hardware support (fingerprint)
Hardware decoder instances are limited by the platform (a few at once on many devices)
Frames must be closed (VideoFrame.close()) or memory fills quickly
Safari support arrived at 16.4 for video; AudioEncoder later
No access to camera without getUserMedia

access.persistence: While objects live
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Available in workers; no iframe flag

capabilities.name: WebRTC data channels (peer to peer)
capabilities.plain: Sends data directly between browsers without a server, with no prompt.
capabilities.meaning: A site can connect two people peer to peer. Setup exchanges network candidates, which can expose the person's public IP address to the other peer or to the site.

limits.headline: Can send data straight between two browsers, with no pop up
limits.user_action: Nothing for data. A video call asks for camera permission only when you use it.
can: Send text, files or game moves straight to another person's browser
Keep the connection open while the pages are open
Connect two people through a quick set up over the internet
cannot: Reach your camera or microphone without a separate permission
Stay connected after you close the page
Work with no server at all; a server helps the two browsers meet
Always hide your network address from the other person

story.what_it_is: Two browsers can send data straight to each other, with no prompt.

marketing.name: WebRTC
marketing.pitch: The WebRTC project says it brings real time communication to browsers through simple APIs.

story.for_you: You never see it. In a video call or a browser game, your device may talk directly to another person's device. That can reveal your network address to the other side.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for real time speed and to save server costs. It powers file sharing, games and calls. It can also expose your real network address even behind a VPN, which fraud teams use to spot you.

use_cases.example: A browser multiplayer game sends player moves directly between players for low delay.
A video call app sends your voice and video peer to peer when it can.
A web file sharing tool sends a large file straight to a friend with no upload.
A live Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW stream uses the same family of tech to send the picture.
A fraud tool uses it to learn a visitor's real network address and spot a VPN.
A shared code editor syncs edits straight between teammates.

technical_bounds: No prompt for data-only connections; camera or mic needs getUserMedia
Local IP candidates hidden behind mDNS .local names (Chrome 75, Safari 11, Firefox 78) unless media permission is granted
STUN reveals the public IP to peers and to the STUN server
Max message size: Chrome about 256 KiB, Firefox up to 1 GiB (maxMessageSize)
Ordered or unordered, reliable or partially reliable; SCTP over DTLS

abuse: Peer to peer botnet or proxy networks

history.change: mDNS host candidates hide local IPs

access.persistence: Lives with the peer connection
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: No iframe flag; permissions policy applies only to camera and microphone
steps: Create RTCPeerConnection with STUN or TURN
Exchange SDP and ICE candidates via signaling

capabilities.name: WebSockets
capabilities.plain: Opens a two-way live connection to a server, with no prompt.
capabilities.meaning: A site can keep a persistent channel to its server for chat, live data or telemetry. It is not covered by CORS, and the connection ends when the tab closes.

limits.headline: Can keep a live two way link to a server, with no pop up
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, like chat, live scores or games.
can: Send and get messages in both directions at once
Keep the link open while the page is open
Update the page right away with new data
cannot: Stay connected after you close the tab
Reach your files or other apps
Keep running well in a hidden tab; browsers may slow or drop it

story.what_it_is: A page can keep a live two way line open to a server, with no prompt.

marketing.name: WebSockets API
marketing.pitch: MDN says WebSockets let a page and a server send messages back and forth without repeated requests.

story.for_you: You never see it. Chat messages, live scores and multiplayer moves arrive the instant they happen, with no refresh.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for anything live: chat, trading, games, dashboards. It keeps a steady line open, which is faster than asking again and again.

use_cases.example: A browser shooter or io game sends your position to the server and gets everyone else's back many times a second.
A chat app delivers a message the second someone sends it.
A trading page streams live prices and fills.
Twitch chat flows through a live connection, so messages appear as they happen.
A shared doc editor sends every keystroke to teammates in real time.
A fraud tool streams behaviour signals from a login page to a scoring server as you type.

technical_bounds: Origin header is sent but no CORS check: servers must validate Origin
Mixed content: ws:// from an HTTPS page is blocked (Chrome, Firefox, Safari)
Per-host connection limits: Firefox 200 (network.websocket.max-connections); Chrome around 255 per renderer
Blocked ports list (about 70 ports such as 25, 110, 6667) applies
No backpressure in the classic API (messages buffer in bufferedAmount)
Closed when the tab goes into BFCache and not reconnected automatically

abuse: Cross-site WebSocket hijacking when Origin unchecked

history.change: WebSocket origin check for localhost still permitted

platform.api: new WebSocket('wss://...'); WebSocketStream (Chrome origin trial history)

access.persistence: Lives with the page; closed on unload; BFCache closes it
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Governed by CSP connect-src; no iframe flag needed
steps: Browser performs HTTP upgrade with Origin header

capabilities.name: WebTransport
capabilities.plain: Opens low-latency streams and datagrams to an HTTP/3 server, with no prompt.
capabilities.meaning: A site can send and receive many parallel streams and unreliable datagrams over QUIC. Faster than WebSockets, but also a flexible channel for covert upload.

limits.headline: Can open fast two way streams to a server, with no pop up
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads, like a live video or game.
can: Send and get many streams of data at once
Send small quick messages with low delay
Keep the link open while the page is open
cannot: Work with a server that does not support HTTP/3
Stay connected after you close the tab
Work in Safari, including on iPhone, where it is not available yet
Reach your files or other apps
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox support it. Safari does not yet.

story.what_it_is: A newer, faster live line to a server, with no prompt.

marketing.name: WebTransport
marketing.pitch: Chrome's docs say WebTransport offers low delay two way streams and datagrams over HTTP/3.

story.for_you: You never see it. It makes cloud games, live video and fast apps feel quicker, especially on shaky wifi.
story.for_makers: Makers get lower delay than older live lines and can send things out of order, which is perfect for games where old data is useless. It is the next step beyond WebSockets.

use_cases.example: A cloud game or a fast browser shooter sends controller and move data as quick datagrams, so a lost packet does not stall the game.
A live sports stream delivers video with sub second delay.
A conferencing tool sends media over HTTP/3 and recovers faster from poor networks.
A shared whiteboard syncs strokes with very low delay.
A telemetry tool streams many small events without blocking.
A remote desktop in the browser streams the screen and input at low delay.

story.for_you: You drag a file from your desktop onto the page and let go. It is the act of dropping that gives the page the file. No prompt appears because you did it yourself.
story.for_makers: It is the easiest way to add files and feels natural. Makers get fast uploads and fewer clicks. Because the drop is the consent, no extra prompt is needed.

use_cases.example: You drop a picture or document into a chat window to send it.
You drop a photo into a web editor to start work.
You drop files into a cloud folder in your browser.
You drop a save file or custom map onto a browser game to load it.
You drag a file onto an email to attach it.
You drop a video onto an online converter or editor.
You drop a folder of files onto a web deploy tool.

risks: Easy to drop the wrong file

technical_bounds: Contents readable only inside the drop handler (protected mode otherwise)
Dropped folders: webkitGetAsEntry returns the full tree, readEntries returns at most 100 entries per call in Chrome (loop until empty)
getAsFileSystemHandle (Chrome 86) can request write access to the dropped file with a prompt
Cannot start a drag from OS file locations; cannot read drag data before drop
Dropped item paths are hidden; only names and relative paths

platform.api: drop event; dataTransfer.files; items; webkitGetAsEntry(); getAsFileSystemHandle()

access.persistence: Per drop
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Drops go to the document under the pointer; dropped items are same-origin readable only in that document
steps: Person drags files from the OS
Page reads files and walks directory entries

capabilities.meaning: The most common way a site reaches a person's files. The person picks exactly what is shared, and the site sees name, size, type and modified time, but not the folder path.

Upload them to its servers
See their name, size and type

story.what_it_is: Opens your system's file chooser, and the page gets only the files you pick.

marketing.name: input type file
marketing.pitch: Documents the standard way a page asks a person to choose files to share.

story.for_you: You tap 'Choose file', pick a photo or document in a system window, and the page gets only that one. It cannot see anything else on your device.
story.for_makers: It is the safest, oldest way to get files. It works everywhere with no permission pop up, which is why upload forms are built on it.

use_cases.example: You pick a profile photo from your camera roll.
You choose a PDF statement to upload to a loan application.
You choose an essay file to submit to a class.
You choose a file to attach to a message.
You pick a scan or lab result to share with a clinic.
You pick a profile avatar or a custom skin for a browser game.
You pick a photo to send for a return request.

technical_bounds: Can open the picker only from a click, tap or key press (input.showPicker also needs activation)
The path is hidden: value shows C:\fakepath\name; no folder, no sibling files
Cannot set files programmatically to a chosen path; only via DataTransfer from existing File objects
Reads the file as it is at read time; later edits throw NotReadableError in Chrome and Safari if the file changed
accept filter is a hint, not enforcement; no size limit from the browser (memory bound)

abuse: Tricking people into uploading private files
Reading photo metadata (GPS EXIF) from uploads

history.change: HTMLInputElement.showPicker() ships, so a script can open the chooser from its own gesture handler

marketing.name: File API
marketing.pitch: Documents how a page can read basic details of a file a person has chosen.

story.for_you: The page sees the name, size, kind and last changed time of each file you give it. You never see it read, but it is why an upload checks the size first.

A loan portal checks that your uploads are PDFs or photos, not other file types.
A fraud team reads the last changed time of an uploaded ID photo to see if it was just edited.
A mod site checks the name and size of a mod file for known cheats.
A music tool reads the file name and type to pick a sound format.
A homework site checks that the file was last changed before the deadline.
A document system uses the last changed time to decide which copy is newer.

A music tool opens a project file and writes the changes without making a copy.

A company web app edits spreadsheets in place on a shared drive.

capabilities.meaning: A site can store large files and databases on disk invisibly to the person. It is sandboxed per site, but it can fill gigabytes of disk and survives until site data is cleared.

limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the app stores data such as a database or editor project.

Do all this with no prompt

story.for_makers: It gives web apps fast, real file access without a prompt. That makes serious tools possible, such as databases and editors in the browser. It counts toward your storage quota.

use_cases.example: A browser game keeps its large levels and save files here so loading is fast.
A web photo or video editor keeps its working files here so edits are quick.
A web database like SQLite runs in the browser and stores its data here.
A note app keeps a full offline copy of your notes in this space.
A video tool keeps a big clip here while you edit it.
A malicious site could fill this space with junk. Browsers limit the size.
A tracking script could keep a hidden ID file here that cookie clearing may not remove.

capabilities.name: Spoofing and lie detection (signals)
capabilities.plain: Checks whether language, resolution, OS or browser values were faked and whether an ad blocker is on.
capabilities.meaning: Compares claimed values with probed ones to spot people using privacy tools or anti-detect browsers. The result becomes a fingerprint signal in itself.

limits.headline: Can check whether your browser settings were faked or an ad blocker is on
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: Compare your claimed language, screen size and system with what the browser actually shows
Tell if an ad blocker is running

story.what_it_is: A script checks whether your browser's reported language, screen or system were faked, and whether an ad blocker is on.
story.for_you: You never see it. The site quietly checks that the story your browser tells is consistent. If it looks faked, you may get an extra check, a CAPTCHA, or a blocked checkout with no clear reason.
story.for_makers: Fraud and bot teams use it to catch people who hide behind fake settings. Ad networks use it to spot ad blockers and bots. It also lets trackers notice who is trying to avoid them.

use_cases.example: A fraud tool sees a browser claiming to be an iPhone but acting like a Linux server, and flags it as a bot.
Fraud checks compare your reported time zone, language and device. A mismatch can send an order for manual review.
An ad network tests for fake traffic. If the browser lies about its screen size, the click is not billed to the advertiser.
A free to play browser game bans players who fake their device to farm rewards many times.
A news site detects an ad blocker and shows a polite wall asking you to turn it off or subscribe.
A ticket site spots scalper bots that fake many different devices to grab seats, and lets real fans through.
Analytics tools filter out visits where values were spoofed, so charts are not full of fake visitors.

risks: Can single out people who hide

technical_bounds: Cannot tell which tool caused the mismatch

A measurement vendor keeps traffic counts clean by excluding visits with no trust mark.

capabilities.name: Client IP address
capabilities.plain: Every request carries the sender's public IP address.
capabilities.meaning: The server sees the IP (or the proxy or relay address). IPv4 gives about 32 bits at most; an IPv6 /64 gives up to 64. It is the base for geolocation, ISP and VPN checks, and rate limits. Shared NAT and CGNAT blur it.

limits.headline: Can see the public internet address your connection uses
limits.user_action: Nothing. Every site you visit gets it when you connect
can: See your IP address, or your VPN, proxy or relay address
Guess your country and city from it
Check your internet company and spot VPNs
Limit how many requests one address can make
cannot: Find your street address or name
See your device's private home network address
Be sure it is you; shared connections and carrier networks blur it

story.what_it_is: Every site you visit sees your internet address.
story.for_you: You never see it, but every site you visit receives your network address. It shows your internet provider and rough area. A VPN or relay swaps it for another address.
story.for_makers: Makers need it to send you the page. They also use it for rough location, rate limits, abuse blocking and fraud, and ads use it to link visits from the same home or office.

use_cases.example: A multiplayer game server uses your address to place you in a region and connect you with nearby players.
A cloud gaming service uses your address to pick the closest data center for the lowest lag.
A streaming service uses it to decide which shows are licensed in your country.
A website blocks an address that tries a password thousands of times.
An ad network links visits from one household address to guess that devices belong together.
A site counts unique visitors and cities by address.
A bank flags a login from an address it has never seen for that customer.

technical_bounds: Hidden by VPN, Tor, iCloud Private Relay, Chrome IP Protection and corporate proxies
CGNAT shares one IP among hundreds of users

value.legit_uses: Rate limiting, abuse prevention, geo compliance
value.abuse: Cross-site tracking when combined with other signals

platform.api: TCP/IP source address; X-Forwarded-For at proxies

steps: Server reads the socket peer address
Join with GeoIP and ASN databases

capabilities.name: DNS resolver leak test
capabilities.plain: A page makes the browser look up unique hostnames so the site learns which DNS resolver the visitor uses.
capabilities.meaning: The page requests random-subdomain.example. The authoritative server logs which recursive resolver asked, revealing the ISP, a public DNS (Google, Cloudflare), or a VPN leak. DoH hides it from the local network, not from the site.

limits.headline: Can find which DNS service your device uses by having it look up odd names
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads in the background
can: Make your browser look up unique made up site names
See which DNS service answers, such as your ISP, Google or Cloudflare
Spot a VPN that leaks DNS
cannot: See which sites you visit in other tabs from this test
Be hidden by encrypted DNS, which only hides it from your network, not from the site
Learn your name from it

story.what_it_is: A page makes your browser look up odd web names so it can see which DNS service you use.
story.for_you: You see nothing. The page quietly asks your browser to look up random names, and the site's own server sees which DNS service asked. That can show your internet provider or whether a VPN is leaking.
story.for_makers: VPN, privacy and security testers use it to check leaks. Fraud teams can use it as one more clue to where you really are, even behind a VPN.

use_cases.example: A VPN leak test website shows which DNS service your computer uses, and whether it matches the VPN.
A fraud system compares the DNS service with the claimed country and flags a mismatch.
A game anti cheat or region lock service checks whether a player behind a VPN is faking a region.
A streaming service checks for DNS tricks used to unlock other regions.
A privacy researcher measures which DNS services people use.
A tracker can use the resolver as an extra clue to link visits.

technical_bounds: ECS (EDNS client subnet) may leak a client prefix
Resolver may not map to a person

value.abuse: VPN bypass detection, network profiling

history.change: Automatic DoH upgrade for supporting resolvers

platform.api: fetch/img to unique subdomains; authoritative DNS logging

steps: Compare to client IP and VPN claim

capabilities.name: ECH and DoH visibility
capabilities.plain: Encrypted Client Hello and DNS over HTTPS hide which site a visitor connects to from the local network.
capabilities.meaning: ECH encrypts the SNI and the rest of the ClientHello using a key from DNS HTTPS records (RFC 9849 in Chrome 117 and Firefox 118 era). DoH encrypts DNS lookups. They hide hostnames from ISPs but not from the site, and they weaken JA3/JA4 on the wire.

limits.headline: Can hide the site you visit from your internet provider, not from the site itself
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser can turn it on by itself, or you choose it in settings
can: Hide the site name from your internet provider on supported sites
Hide your DNS lookups from your network with secure DNS
Keep working on supported sites without changing how pages look
cannot: Hide you from the site you visit; it still sees you connect
Work in Safari today
Work with some network filters and monitors, which may break or block it
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Samsung Internet support it. Safari does not yet.

story.what_it_is: Hides which site you connect to from people watching your network.

marketing.name: Encrypted Client Hello
marketing.pitch: Cloudflare pitches it as the missing piece that hides which website you visit from anyone watching the connection.

marketing.name: DNS over HTTPS
marketing.pitch: Mozilla describes DNS over HTTPS as a way to encrypt website lookups so others on the network cannot see them.

story.for_you: You see nothing change. On public Wi-Fi or at a school, the network can no longer easily see which site you are opening. Your home network or work can still see that you connected.
story.for_makers: Makers get stronger privacy for visitors and fewer blocked connections. Network filters, schools and countries lose an easy way to block sites by name. Some security tools also lose visibility.

use_cases.example: A news site in a country with censorship becomes harder for the network to block by name.
A gamer on school or hotel Wi-Fi opens a game site that the network blocks by name, and it still loads.
A company security tool loses sight of which sites staff open, so it uses managed browsers instead.
A shopper on cafe Wi-Fi hides which stores they visit from nearby snoopers.
Internet providers lose a data source used to sell browsing history to marketers.
A researcher measures how much web traffic hides its destination.

technical_bounds: Needs an ECH enabled CDN (Cloudflare) and DoH
Outer SNI still visible as a shared public name

value.abuse: Makes middlebox TLS fingerprinting harder

platform.api: TLS ECH extension; HTTPS RR; DoH

steps: Network sees only a public name

capabilities.name: ETag and HTTP cache supercookie
capabilities.plain: A tracker stores an ID in the cache validators of a file, which come back on every request.
capabilities.meaning: A server sets a unique ETag or Last-Modified on a resource; the browser sends If-None-Match back, identifying the visitor. Since cache partitioning (Chrome 86, Firefox 85, Safari earlier) the ID is only valid per top-level site.

limits.headline: Can try to tag your browser with a hidden cached ID, though browsers now limit it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit a site that tries it
can: Store an ID in the cache details of a file
Recognise a returning visitor on the same site
Keep the ID after you clear cookies in older browsers
cannot: Follow you across different sites; modern browsers separate the cache by site
Survive clearing your cache or browsing data
Work the same in every browser
limits.differs: Chrome, Firefox and Safari all split the cache by site now, so the ID only works inside one site.

story.what_it_is: A tracker hides a personal ID in a saved file's label, so it survives clearing cookies.

marketing.name: HTTP cache partitioning
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes splitting the cache by site so one site cannot learn about your visits to another through shared cached files.

story.for_you: You never see it. You clear your cookies and still get recognized, because the ID rides on a cached file. Modern browsers now keep separate caches per site, which weakens this trick.
story.for_makers: Trackers and ad firms used it as a backup when cookies were blocked or deleted. It is mostly unfriendly to privacy, and browsers have been closing it with split caches.

use_cases.example: An ad network labels a tiny image with a unique tag and reads it back to recognize you on the next visit.
An analytics script rebuilds a lost ID from the cache label after cookies are cleared.
A fraud company uses it to link a returning bot or a banned account.
A retargeting service recognizes a shopper who deleted cookies and shows the same product ads.
A game portal links a banned player's new browser session to the old one.
A video site recognizes a viewer who tried to dodge a free article limit.

technical_bounds: Cross-site ID no longer works; same-site ID still works
Cleared with Clear browsing data

value.abuse: Cookie free first party tracking

steps: Later request sends If-None-Match with the ID

capabilities.name: Favicon cache supercookie (F-CACHE)
capabilities.plain: A site encodes an ID into which favicons were cached, which survives clearing cookies.
capabilities.meaning: NDSS 2021 (Solomos et al.) showed a persistent ID stored in the favicon cache across subdomains, surviving cookie clearing and even private browsing in some browsers. Vendors patched after disclosure.

limits.headline: Can try to tag your browser with a hidden icon cache ID, though fixes limit it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit a site that tries it
can: Store an ID using which tiny site icons your browser has cached
Recognise a returning visitor, even after you clear cookies in unpatched browsers
Link visits across subdomains of the same site in older versions
cannot: Work in browsers that fixed it after researchers reported it in 2021
Follow you across unrelated sites
Survive clearing browsing data in updated browsers
limits.differs: Browser makers patched it after 2021, so behavior differs by version.

story.what_it_is: A site hides an ID in which tiny page icons your browser has saved.
story.for_you: You never see it. You clear cookies and history, and a site still knows it is you, because of the pattern of tiny icons your browser saved. Browsers have worked to close this.
story.for_makers: Researchers showed it works across subdomains and even in private mode. A tracker could use it as a persistent ID. Makers who care about privacy prefer to avoid it, and browsers are closing the hole.

use_cases.example: A tracking network sets a pattern of favicons on a first visit and reads it back later to recognize you.
A measurement script reconnects returning visitors who cleared cookies.
A fraud tool uses it to link accounts from one browser even in private windows.
A marketing site recognizes a shopper who tries to look anonymous.
A game site could link a banned user to a new account made in the same browser.
A publisher could count one reader as one person across paywall resets.

technical_bounds: Patched in Chrome, Safari and Brave (reported)
Needs many subdomains and requests

value.abuse: Cookie-free persistent tracking, survives incognito in affected builds

history.change: Solomos et al. Tracking You Persistently via Favicons (NDSS 2021)

refs.label: Solomos et al., Tracking You Persistently via Favicons (NDSS 2021)

platform.api: Favicon requests to N subdomain paths; navigation redirect probing

steps: Load pages with chosen favicons to write bits

capabilities.name: HSTS supercookie
capabilities.plain: A site stores an ID in which subdomains the browser has been told to load only over HTTPS.
capabilities.meaning: Each bit is a subdomain set to HSTS or not. The tracker reads it back by probing http:// URLs and seeing which upgrade (Kamkar 2015). Safari's ITP and clearing site data restrict it; HSTS is mostly cleared with history.

data.metric: N bit identifier (a few dozen subdomains)

limits.headline: Can try to tag your browser with a hidden secure site ID, though it is limited
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit a site that tries it
can: Store bits by choosing which subdomains your browser forces onto https
Check them later by trying plain http web addresses
Recognise a returning visitor until you clear history or site data
cannot: Survive clearing history in most browsers
Work well in Safari, which limits it
Carry much data; each subdomain gives one bit
limits.reach_label: Small ID, mostly cleared by history
limits.differs: Safari limits it. Chrome, Edge and Firefox allow it partly, but it is cleared with history.

story.what_it_is: A site stores an ID in which of its sub-sites your browser forces onto secure mode.
story.for_you: You never see it. Your browser remembers secure site choices. A tracker can set many tiny secure flags like switches and read them back later to see your personal code. Many browsers now limit this trick.
story.for_makers: It is an old trick to recognize people after cookie clearing, and it still shapes how browsers handle secure site lists. Trackers once used it. Privacy teams want it blocked.

use_cases.example: A tracker sets a pattern of secure site flags on a first visit and reads it back to recognize you.
An analytics vendor uses it as a backup ID when cookies are deleted.
A researcher shows how it could re identify private browsing users.
A store ad partner uses it to re identify a shopper who cleared cookies.
A publisher could match a returning reader behind a paywall.
A game site could link repeat sessions of a banned player.

technical_bounds: Needs dozens of subdomains and many requests
Cleared when the person clears browsing data

value.abuse: Cookie-free persistent ID

history.change: WebKit limits HSTS to prevent cross-site tracking (ITP)

steps: Set HSTS on chosen subdomains to write bits
Check which redirect to https to read the ID

capabilities.name: HTTP header order and casing
capabilities.plain: The set and order of request headers is different for each browser and HTTP library.
capabilities.meaning: Chrome, Firefox and Safari send Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding and Sec-* headers in distinct orders; scripted clients (requests, Go, Node fetch) differ. Mismatches versus the User-Agent flag bots.

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from the order of request headers
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens with every page request
can: Compare the order and casing of header lines with known browsers
Spot scripts and bots that use plain code libraries
Flag a browser name that does not match the headers
cannot: Know your name or account from it
See your files or other tabs
Tell two people on the same browser version apart

story.what_it_is: The order of the info your browser sends to a site reveals which browser it is.
story.for_you: You never see it. Each browser sends the same pieces in a slightly different order, like a signature. A site can tell Chrome from Firefox from a script even if the browser claims otherwise.
story.for_makers: Bot defense vendors use header order as a quick way to catch scripts pretending to be browsers. It is also a fingerprint input, since software versions and add-ons leave marks.

use_cases.example: A bot defense checks if the header order matches the browser claim, and blocks scripts that fake Chrome.
A game login page blocks credential stuffing tools that send headers in an odd order.
A sneaker or ticket site spots scalper bots by header order before the sale begins.
An ad platform filters click fraud from scripts with the wrong header signature.
A traffic report separates real browsers from crawlers.
A streaming site stops account sharing and scraping tools by headers.

technical_bounds: Proxies and CDNs can reorder headers
HTTP/2 lowercases names

value.abuse: Client identification

capabilities.name: HTTP/2 connection fingerprint (Akamai)
capabilities.plain: HTTP/2 settings, window updates and header order differ by browser and are readable by the server.
capabilities.meaning: Akamai's fingerprint (Black Hat EU 2017) joins SETTINGS values, WINDOW_UPDATE, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order. Chrome sends m,a,s,p, Firefox m,p,a,s and Safari m,s,p,a; Go and Python clients differ visibly.

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from how your connection starts up
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as your browser connects to the site
can: Compare connection settings and header order with known browsers
Tell Chrome, Firefox and Safari apart from each other
Spot scripts and bots whose settings look different
cannot: Know your name or account from it
Tell two people on the same browser apart
Apply to old HTTP/1.1 connections

story.what_it_is: The way your browser opens a modern web connection leaves a signature the site can read.
story.for_you: You never see it. When you connect, your browser sends settings in a pattern that is almost the same for every copy of Chrome, Safari or Firefox. A site can tell the real thing from a lookalike script.
story.for_makers: Security vendors like Akamai and Cloudflare use it to tell real browsers from bots that fake a browser name. It catches many scrapers and card testing tools. It also adds to a fingerprint that is hard to change.

use_cases.example: A bot defense compares the connection pattern with the claimed browser and challenges mismatches.
A retailer stops price scrapers that pretend to be Chrome.
A game launcher site blocks automated tools that buy limited items.
An ad platform removes fake traffic from automation tools.
A bank adds the connection pattern to its fraud score at login.
A traffic analyst uses it to name the real browser share.

technical_bounds: Spoofable by custom HTTP stacks
Same fingerprint across browser versions sharing an engine

value.abuse: Cross-session client identification

refs.label: Shuster et al., Passive Fingerprinting of HTTP/2 Clients (Black Hat EU 2017)

platform.api: HTTP/2 frame capture at the edge

capabilities.name: HTTP/3 and QUIC fingerprint
capabilities.plain: QUIC's first packet carries a readable ClientHello, giving the same fingerprints as TLS plus transport parameters.
capabilities.meaning: The QUIC Initial packet is encrypted with a public key, so middleboxes can read the TLS ClientHello and QUIC transport parameters. JA4 has a QUIC variant (prefix q). Connection ID length and version also differ per stack.

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from the first packet of a fast connection
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your browser opens a new HTTP/3 connection
can: Compare the opening packet and its settings with known browsers
Use the same kind of fingerprint as normal secure connections
Spot scripts and bots with unusual connection details
cannot: Know your name or account from it
Tell two people on the same browser apart
Apply to sites that do not use HTTP/3

story.what_it_is: The first packet of the newest connection type shows readable clues about your browser.
story.for_you: You never see it. When your browser starts a fast new type of connection, the first message has readable details that match your browser and system. A server can tell real browsers from fake ones.
story.for_makers: Bot defense and fraud teams extend their older checks to the newest connection type. It gives them the same browser signature plus extra transport details. It also adds to a long term fingerprint.

use_cases.example: A bot defense reads the first packet and blocks tools that fake a browser name.
A game portal blocks cheat sellers that script account creation.
A retailer protects limited drops from bots.
A video site blocks scrapers that rip its streams.
An ad network filters click farms by connection pattern.
A researcher measures which browsers use the new connection type.

technical_bounds: Less deployed than TCP fingerprints
ECH will hide inner ClientHello fields

value.abuse: Same as JA4

history.change: RFC 9000 and 9001 define QUIC and its TLS binding

platform.api: QUIC Initial packet decrypt at edge; JA4 q variant

capabilities.name: IP geolocation
capabilities.plain: The server converts the visitor's IP into an approximate country, region and city.
capabilities.meaning: Commercial databases (MaxMind, IPinfo, IP2Location) map IPs to places. Vendors claim about 99.8% country accuracy, but city accuracy is much lower and mobile or VPN IPs often point to the carrier hub or exit.

data.metric: Country, region, city, lat and long with accuracy radius

fields.name: accuracy radius
fields.precision: city level in good cases, vendor reported

limits.headline: Can guess your country, region and city from your IP address
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device connects to the site
can: Look up a likely country, region and city from your IP
Show local content, prices and language
Spot a mismatch with your time zone, such as when you use a VPN
cannot: Find your street or home; city guesses are much less exact than country
Get it right on mobile and VPN connections, which often point to a carrier hub or exit
Know your name or account from it
limits.reach_label: Country is close, city is rough

story.what_it_is: A site turns your internet address into a guess of your country, region and city.
story.for_you: You never have to allow anything. Sites guess your country and often your city from your internet address. It is right for countries most of the time, less for cities. A VPN changes the guess.
story.for_makers: Makers use it for local prices, language, taxes and rights. Ads use it for regional targeting. Fraud teams compare it with your billing address and sign in history.

use_cases.example: A game site picks your server region and shows local store prices.
A cloud gaming service uses it to see which data center is close to you and whether the game is licensed in your country.
A streaming service uses it to show only the shows allowed in your country.
A store shows prices, taxes and delivery for your country.
An ad network shows local ads for your city, such as nearby store offers.
A bank flags a login from a country the customer has never visited.
A site measures where its readers live without asking them.

technical_bounds: City accuracy varies widely and is often wrong for mobile and VPN users
Does not reveal street address

value.legit_uses: Content localization, tax and licensing, fraud rules
value.abuse: Price discrimination, geoblocking, stalking via leaked city

capabilities.name: IP masking (Private Relay, IP Protection, Tor)
capabilities.plain: Some browsers route traffic through relays so sites do not see the visitor's real IP.
capabilities.meaning: iCloud Private Relay (Safari, iCloud+ subscribers) uses two hops with a coarse egress location. Chrome IP Protection proxies selected third-party traffic in Incognito for known trackers. Tor routes everything over 3 hops.

limits.headline: Can see only a relay's address when you browse with Private Relay, IP Protection or Tor
limits.user_action: You turn on iCloud Private Relay, use Tor Browser, or browse in Chrome Incognito with IP Protection
can: See the relay's internet address instead of your home address
Guess your rough area from the coarse location a relay shares
Treat relay traffic as higher risk and ask extra questions or block it
cannot: Learn your real home address when the relay is working
Tell that a relay is in use with certainty, since a site can only guess from known relay lists
Get this from Firefox, which has no built in relay feature
Break the relay for you; the protection stays on until you switch it off
limits.differs: Private Relay is Safari with iCloud+; IP Protection is limited to Chrome Incognito and known trackers; Firefox has no built in relay.

story.what_it_is: Some browsers and services hide your real internet address behind a relay so sites see a different one.

marketing.name: iCloud Private Relay
marketing.pitch: Sends your browsing through two relays so no single party knows both who you are and which sites you visit.

marketing.name: Tor Browser
marketing.pitch: Bounces your traffic through volunteer servers so websites cannot see where you really connect from.

story.for_you: You usually notice nothing. Pages load as normal, but a site may think you are in a nearby city, not your own. Some sites may ask extra questions or block you because your address looks hidden.
story.for_makers: Makers see the relay's address, not the visitor's home address. That breaks easy location guessing, ad targeting by address and per-person rate limits. Teams must decide whether to trust, challenge or block these visitors.

use_cases.example: A Safari user with Private Relay on opens a news site. The site sees a shared regional address, so it shows a broad local edition, not street level local ads.
A player in a browser shooter connects through a relay. The game server sees a relay address, so matchmaking picks a server by relay region and ping can rise a few milliseconds.

Cloud gaming in the browser, such as Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW, checks region before starting. A masked address can show the wrong country or add lag, so the player may be told the service is unavailable.
An ad network normally buys local ads by address. With masking, it only knows the broad area, so it falls back to page topic ads and reports less precise location data.
A bank sees a login from a relay address it has never seen. It may ask for a code by text, because relays hide the usual signals of where the person lives.
A store applies country pricing and tax by address. A masked visitor may see another region's price until they enter a shipping address at checkout.
A site counts unique visitors by address. Many people share one relay address, so the count is lower and the city report is blurrier.

technical_bounds: Only protects against sites, not the relay operator
Relay IPs appear on VPN lists and trigger blocks
Chrome IP Protection covers listed third-party domains only (reported)

value.abuse: Fraud and bot blockers treat relays as high risk

capabilities.name: IPv6 prefix and interface ID stability
capabilities.plain: IPv6 addresses can stay stable for weeks, making them a long lived ID even if cookies are cleared.
capabilities.meaning: The /64 prefix delegated by an ISP often persists for weeks or months, while privacy extensions rotate the interface ID (about daily). Servers key on the /64 or /56 to identify a household.

limits.headline: Can tell your home network apart by its stable IPv6 address, even after clearing cookies
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device loads a page over IPv6
can: See the first half of your IPv6 address, which often stays the same for weeks or months
Recognize the same household again after you clear cookies
Use it to limit how many requests one home can make
cannot: Tell which person or device at home is browsing from the stable part alone
Follow you once you move to a different network, such as a cafe or mobile data
Follow the second half of the address for long, since devices change it about daily
Work for you if your connection is IPv4 only

story.what_it_is: Your IPv6 internet address can stay the same for weeks, so it can quietly work like a long lived ID.
story.for_you: You never see this. Your home network is given a long lasting address block, and every site you visit can see the same front part of it. Clearing cookies does not change it.
story.for_makers: Makers can link visits from the same home even when cookies are gone. It is cheap and works for every request. Privacy extensions rotate part of the address, but the network prefix often stays put.

use_cases.example: An ad network sees the same home network prefix across three different news sites. It treats the visits as one household and shows follow up ads even though cookies were cleared.
A shop's fraud system sees a new account come from the same IPv6 prefix as ten banned accounts. It holds the order for review.
A browser game bans a cheater by network prefix. The player who clears cookies and makes a new account still gets blocked because the prefix matches.
An analytics tool uses the prefix, plus browser clues, to stitch a repeat visitor across weeks when cookies are blocked.
A social site spots many fake accounts created from one household prefix and limits sign ups from it.
A streaming site limits how many devices can play at once per household and uses the network prefix to tell which devices share a home.
A company login portal trusts a staff member's home prefix as a familiar place, and asks for less proof from it.

technical_bounds: Privacy extensions rotate the interface ID, not the prefix
Mobile carriers change prefix more often

value.abuse: Household level tracking

refs.label: RFC 7721 Security and privacy of IPv6 addressing

capabilities.name: JA3 TLS client fingerprint
capabilities.plain: The TLS handshake order of ciphers and extensions identifies the client software.
capabilities.meaning: JA3 (Salesforce, 2017) is an MD5 of version, ciphers, extensions, curves and point formats in the ClientHello. Chrome 110 randomized extension order (Jan 2023), so one browser now yields many JA3s; JA4 sorts them out.

fields.name: ja3_hash
fields.precision: exact, but unstable on Chrome 110 and later

limits.headline: Can guess which browser or app you use from how your connection starts
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens the moment your browser connects to the site
can: Make a short code from the list of options your browser offers when it connects
Spot bots, scripts and malware that connect differently from real browsers
Recognize the same software again across different internet addresses
cannot: See your name, account or what you browse
Give one steady code for Chrome, since Chrome shuffles the order and gives many codes
Be turned off in your browser settings
Tell two people with identical software apart
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge shuffle the options on purpose, so one browser gives many codes. Firefox and Safari keep a steadier order.

story.what_it_is: The way your browser starts a secure connection leaves a pattern that names the software you use.
story.for_you: You never see it. Before any page loads, your browser says hello in a particular order. Servers can turn that order into a short code that points to your browser family.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to tell real Chrome or Safari apart from scripts and bots pretending to be them. It happens before any page code runs, so it is hard to fake. Browsers now shuffle the order, which weakens it.

use_cases.example: A ticket site gets a flood of requests that say they are Chrome. The secure handshake code matches a Python script, so the site blocks them before the sale opens.
An ad network checks that clicks come from real browsers. Clicks with a known bot handshake code are dropped and not billed to the advertiser.
A browser game's login server blocks a cheating tool that automates logins, because its handshake matches a known tool and not a normal browser.
A sneaker store uses the handshake code to spot buying bots that fake a browser name, so real shoppers get a fairer chance.
A bot defence service lists the most common handshake codes in its traffic and sets alarms when a rare one suddenly appears.
A bank's login page treats a handshake that does not match the claimed browser as a warning sign and adds a challenge.
A developer scraping a site with a plain script gets blocked, and learns the site compares the handshake code with the browser name sent.

technical_bounds: Chrome randomization makes the hash non-stable
Easy to spoof with curl-impersonate or uTLS

value.abuse: Persistent client identification across IPs

history.change: TLS extension order randomized, breaking static JA3 hashes

platform.api: TLS ClientHello parsing at CDN or server

capabilities.name: JA4+ network fingerprint family
capabilities.plain: A newer family of fingerprints for TLS, HTTP, TCP and more, built to survive randomization.
capabilities.meaning: JA4 (FoxIO, 2023) sorts ciphers and extensions so Chrome's shuffle gives one value. JA4S (server), JA4H (HTTP), JA4L (latency), JA4X (cert), JA4SSH and JA4T (TCP) extend it. JA4 is BSD licensed; the rest use FoxIO License 1.1.

limits.headline: Can recognize your browser or app from several quiet network clues, even when shuffled
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device connects and sends requests
can: Build a sorted code from how your browser starts a connection, so shuffling does not hide it
Add clues from the web request, connection timing and certificates
Use the codes to block bots and hunt for attacks
Keep tracking the same client across different internet addresses
cannot: See who you are by name or account
See page content or what you type
Be switched off from your browser settings
Tell apart two people with the same software and similar setup

story.what_it_is: A newer set of network fingerprints that still names your software, even when browsers shuffle their handshake.
story.for_you: You never see this. Many layers of your connection, from secure handshake to web request, leave small patterns. Together they point to what kind of device and software you use.
story.for_makers: Makers use these codes because they stay useful after browsers randomize order. Defenders share lists of good and bad codes to catch bots and malware. The same data can quietly help sort visitors without cookies.

use_cases.example: A bot defence service sees a login attack that claims to be Safari on iPhone. The network codes match a Linux scripting tool, so it blocks the traffic.
An ad exchange flags fake traffic farms because thousands of visits share one rare network code but claim to be many different phones.
A cloud gaming sign in page rejects automated account sellers whose connection pattern matches a known tool and not a real browser.
A ticket seller keeps a list of codes seen in past scalper attacks and rejects new requests that match them.
A company's security team uses the codes to spot a stolen login coming from a very different kind of device than the owner's laptop.
A threat research team groups web attacks by shared code to find which ones come from the same toolkit.
A bank adds the code to its risk score at login. A match with the customer's usual code lowers friction for them.

technical_bounds: Spoofable by uTLS and curl-impersonate
Software versions share hashes

value.legit_uses: Bot management, threat hunting (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Fastly)
value.abuse: Client tracking

history.change: JA4 and JA4+ announced by FoxIO
Cloudflare exposes JA4 in Bot Management

steps: Hash into a readable a_b_c string

capabilities.name: Local Network Access (LNA) permission
capabilities.plain: Chrome asks the user before a public website can reach devices on their local network.
capabilities.meaning: Chrome 142 added a prompt for requests to private IPs. Chrome 145 split it into local-network and loopback-network permissions, and 147 extended it to WebSocket and WebTransport. It replaced Private Network Access preflights.

limits.headline: Can connect to devices on your home network, only if you allow it in Chrome
limits.user_action: You open a site and tap Allow on Chrome's local network pop up
can: Look for and connect to printers, routers and smart home devices on your network once you allow it
Talk to local helper apps from a public website
Keep this access for the site until you take it back in site settings
cannot: Reach local devices before you tap Allow in Chrome 142 and newer
Work in Firefox or Safari, which do not offer this permission
Get around the pop up; the old silent checks were replaced by it
Reach your network from Chrome on iPhone
limits.differs: Only Chrome and Edge ask. Firefox, Safari and every iPhone browser do not offer this permission.

story.what_it_is: Chrome asks before a public website can talk to devices in your home or office network.

marketing.name: Local Network Access
marketing.pitch: Chrome now asks you first when a public website tries to reach devices on your local network, to stop sneaky probing.

story.for_you: A pop up asks if the site may look for and connect to devices on your local network. If you say no, the site cannot reach your printer, speakers or router. Nothing changes if you say no and do not need that device.
story.for_makers: Makers who build companion web apps for printers, smart speakers or developer tools must now ask first and explain why. It replaces older hidden checks with one clear permission. Sites that never ask lose silent access.

use_cases.example: A web dashboard for a smart home hub finds lights and thermostats on your network. Chrome asks first, then the page controls them from the browser.
A web player offers to send music to speakers in your living room. Chrome asks to find local devices before the speaker list shows up.
A developer opens a public docs site that talks to a tool running on their own network. They approve once so the page can reach it.
A company's cloud admin page connects to an office printer or card reader by its local address, after a one time allow.
A browser game party site lists consoles or PCs on your Wi-Fi so you can start streaming a game to the web page.
A web casting page searches for TVs on your network and asks first, then shows your nearby TVs.
A malicious ad tries to poke your router login. Chrome shows a prompt, which warns you that something odd is happening.

technical_bounds: Only Chromium; Firefox and Safari have no equivalent prompt
Users can accept for the site persistently

value.legit_uses: Local helper apps, smart home dashboards
value.abuse: Local device probing if granted

history.change: Split into local-network and loopback-network (secondary sources)
Extended to WebSocket and WebTransport (secondary sources)

access.prompt_ui: Look for and connect to any device on your local network

capabilities.name: Localhost and LAN port scanning
capabilities.plain: A page probes ports on the visitor's own machine or home network to find running software.
capabilities.meaning: JavaScript uses fetch, WebSocket or image timing to test localhost ports (eBay's 2020 check, Meta Pixel and Yandex on Android in 2025 messaging via localhost). Chrome LNA prompts since 142 and PNA aim to stop this.

limits.headline: Can try to find software running on your own computer, though Chrome now blocks it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page or ad script loads
can: Test whether your computer has certain programs listening, by timing quick requests
Check whether a companion desktop app is installed
Link web activity to an app on the same device
cannot: Do this silently in Chrome 142 and newer, which shows a pop up first
See files or data inside the programs it finds
Reach other devices on your network without the local network pop up
Work on iPhone browsers against apps, which are sandboxed from each other
limits.reach_label: Your own device, if not blocked
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge now ask first. Firefox and Safari still allow the quiet checks, though they only find what a site already expects. Android apps have been caught doing this.

story.what_it_is: A web page quietly checks which programs are running on your own computer or home network.
story.for_you: You never see it. A page you visit can try to connect to your own computer and learn which apps are open. The answer helps a site decide who you are.
story.for_makers: Some sites use it for fraud checks, such as spotting remote control software. Others have used it to collect hidden signals about the visitor. Browsers are adding rules to stop it.

use_cases.example: A bank site checks for common remote access tools on the visitor's machine. If one is running, it blocks the transfer to stop a scam call from taking over.
An ad script tests a list of local ports to build a hidden fingerprint of installed apps, which adds to a profile without cookies.
A browser game tries to connect to a helper app on a local port. If it answers, the game unlocks desktop features for that player.
A messaging web page checks a local port to see if the desktop app is running. If so, it opens chats there and not in the tab.
A developer tool in the browser connects to a helper on localhost to read files, so the site can show them in the page.
A fraud tool on a checkout page watches for debugging or automation tools open on the buyer's computer.
A company portal checks for its security agent on a local port before it lets staff sign in.

technical_bounds: Chrome 142 gates local requests behind a prompt
Firefox and Safari have no prompt yet (unverified at 2026-11)

value.abuse: Fraud detection by eBay, tracking ID bridging, router attacks

history.change: eBay port scanning reported by Nullsweep
Local Mess: Meta and Yandex localhost ID linking on Android disclosed

refs.label: Local Mess (Meta and Yandex localhost tracking) 2025
