capabilities.name: Private Access Tokens and PACT
capabilities.plain: A signed token proves the visitor is probably a real device without revealing who they are.
capabilities.meaning: Privacy Pass (RFC 9576 to 9578) tokens issued after device or account attestation. Apple PAT ships in Safari and Cloudflare Turnstile consumes tokens. PACT was announced on 2026-06-22 by Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla and Shopify; Apple was not listed.

limits.headline: Can check that you are probably a real device without learning who you are
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a site asks your browser to prove it is genuine
can: Receive a signed token showing a real Apple device or account vouched for you
Skip a CAPTCHA or other challenge for you
Accept the same token without knowing which device made it
cannot: Learn your name, device model or account from the token
Track you from token to token, since they are made to be unlinkable
Work in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Samsung Internet today
Prove you are human with certainty, only that a trusted device vouched
limits.differs: Only Safari on Mac and iPhone issues these tokens today. A cross vendor version called PACT was announced in June 2026.

story.what_it_is: A signed token that proves you are probably a real device, without telling the site who you are.

marketing.name: Private Access Tokens
marketing.pitch: Lets sites skip CAPTCHAs by checking quietly that a real Apple device is visiting, without learning who you are.

marketing.name: Private Access Tokens
marketing.pitch: Cloudflare says these tokens remove CAPTCHAs on iPhones and Macs while keeping visitors private.

story.for_you: On supported Apple devices you see fewer puzzles asking you to pick traffic lights. Your phone proves itself in the background. You never see the check.
story.for_makers: Makers get a strong sign that the visitor is a real device, and not a bot farm, with no extra data to store. It cuts fraud and friction. Sites need a provider such as Cloudflare to issue and check tokens.

use_cases.example: A shop behind Cloudflare skips the puzzle for iPhone shoppers, so more people finish checkout and bots still have to solve harder tests.
A browser game's sign up page checks for a real device token, so one person cannot make hundreds of free accounts for cheating.
A social site lets verified devices post and follow right away, and challenges unverified ones with extra steps.
An ad network discounts clicks that come without a token on devices that normally have one, which reduces click fraud.
A login page uses the token to lower friction for real devices and raise it for scripts that try thousands of passwords.
A news site limits scraping by asking for a token before it serves full articles to automated visitors.
A person who finds image puzzles hard to solve gets in with no puzzle, because the device proves itself in the background.

technical_bounds: Issuers can see attestation requests; issuer collusion is the main risk
PACT is only announced; shipping status unverified

value.abuse: Attestation could exclude minority browsers or devices

history.change: RFC 9576 to 9578 Privacy Pass published (Jun 2024 per IETF)
PACT announced by Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, Shopify

platform.api: Privacy Pass PrivateToken challenge in WWW-Authenticate; PAT

safari.note: Private Access Tokens for iOS 16 and macOS 13

capabilities.name: Referer and Origin headers
capabilities.plain: Requests tell the destination site which page the visitor came from.
capabilities.meaning: The default policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin (Chrome 85, Firefox 87) sends only the origin cross-site. Safari has capped cross-site referrers to the origin since 12.1. Full URLs still go same-site.

limits.headline: Can tell which site you came from, usually just the site name, not the page
limits.user_action: You click a link or load a page that pulls in another site's content
can: See the site address you arrived from, such as example.com
See the full page address when you move around inside the same site
Count visits by traffic source for analytics
cannot: See the full page address of another site you left, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari by default
See your browsing history beyond the one step before
Get a referrer if the previous page chose to send none
limits.reach_label: One step back, mostly the site name
limits.differs: Safari has limited cross site referrers to the site name for years. Chrome and Firefox did the same by default around 2020 and 2021.

story.what_it_is: Each request tells the destination which page or site you came from.

marketing.name: Referrer Policy
marketing.pitch: The standard lets sites choose how much of the previous page address is shared when you click a link.

story.for_you: You never see it. When you click a link or a page loads an image, the other site learns where you were. Browsers now trim it to just the site name by default, so you share less than before.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to see which sites and ads send visitors, to block other sites from copying their images, and to guard forms from forged requests. The origin header helps stop cross site attacks.

use_cases.example: A shop sees that many visitors arrive from a blog post. The referrer tells it which blog to thank and which affiliate to pay.
An advertiser reads the referrer to check that clicks came from the sites it paid, and to spot fake sites.
A photo site stops other sites from showing its pictures for free by checking the referrer on image requests.
A banking site checks the origin header on a transfer form. A request coming from another site is rejected as forged.
A browser game portal sees which partner site a player came from, so it can credit the partner and show a matching start screen.
A social site shows a link preview but trims the referrer so private page addresses do not leak to the linked site.
A news site sees visitors from search, social and email, and uses it to pick which subscription offer to show.

technical_bounds: Pages can loosen it with Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url
Never reveals the referring page across origins by default

value.abuse: Leaks of sensitive URLs, search terms

platform.api: Referer and Origin request headers; Referrer-Policy; document.referrer

capabilities.name: Reverse DNS (PTR) of the client IP
capabilities.plain: A reverse lookup of the IP can return an ISP hostname that hints at location or line type.
capabilities.meaning: PTR records such as pool-1-2-3-4.nycmny.fios.verizon.net expose ISP, city codes and sometimes dynamic vs static addressing. Servers do this for logs and bot checks (Googlebot verification).

limits.headline: Can look up your internet address to learn your provider and sometimes your area
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the site's server logs or checks your visit
can: Learn the name your internet provider gave your address
Spot city codes or home versus business lines in that name
Confirm that a visitor claiming to be a search crawler really is one
cannot: Learn your street address or your name
Work when your provider gives no useful name
See through a VPN or relay, which show their own names
Be blocked from your browser, since it happens on the server side

story.what_it_is: A lookup of your internet address can return a name hinting where you are or what line you use.
story.for_you: You never see it. The server may turn your numeric address into a name like a phone company or a school. That name hints at your area or whether you are on a home line or a data center.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to check that crawlers are who they say, to tell home users from servers, and to guess city or company. It is quick, free and needs no cooperation from the browser.

use_cases.example: A site that gets traffic claiming to be Googlebot checks the address name. If it does not end in Google's domain, it is blocked as an impostor.
An ad network uses the name to tell data center traffic from home traffic, and treats data center clicks as likely fake.
An analytics tool shows visits by company name, because staff of a firm browse from an address that names it.
A B2B sales tool spots a visit from a target company and alerts the salesperson.
A game server list blocks cloud hosting names for ranked play, to stop cheat servers and bots.
A video site sees a university address name and offers the campus subscription deal.
A mail or web server logs address names so staff can trace an abuse complaint to the right network owner.

technical_bounds: Many IPs have no PTR
Cloud IPs return generic names

value.abuse: Residential identification

platform.api: DNS PTR lookup for in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa

capabilities.name: Sec-CH-UA low entropy hints and reduced User-Agent
capabilities.plain: Chromium sends brand, mobile flag and platform in every request by default, with a frozen User-Agent string.
capabilities.meaning: Sec-CH-UA lists browser brands and major versions (with a GREASE brand), Sec-CH-UA-Mobile and Sec-CH-UA-Platform. The User-Agent string is frozen to a reduced form in Chrome 110 and later.

limits.headline: Can see your browser brand, major version, phone or computer type, and system in Chromium browsers
limits.user_action: Nothing. Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet send it with every request
can: See your browser brand and its main version number
Tell if you are on a phone or a computer
See your operating system name
Ask for more detail such as exact version or device model, which the browser may then share
cannot: See your exact device model or full version unless it asks and the browser agrees
Get this from Firefox or Safari, which do not send it
See your name or account
Rely on the older browser name string, which is now kept short and generic
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet send it by default. Firefox and Safari, including all iPhone browsers, do not.

story.what_it_is: Chrome based browsers tell every site your browser brand, whether you are on mobile, and your system type.

marketing.name: User-Agent Client Hints
marketing.pitch: Chrome freezes the old browser string and shares details only when a site asks, to cut passive tracking.

story.for_you: You never see it. Each page request includes a short note: your browser brand, if it is a phone, and your platform. A site asks for more detail, such as device model, only if it needs it.
story.for_makers: Makers use the basic note to serve the right layout, the right app download link and the right video format. The old long browser string is frozen, so finer detail needs an extra request, which browsers can limit.

use_cases.example: A video site reads the platform and mobile flag and offers a phone friendly player without any page code running first.
A browser game portal sees you are on a phone and loads touch controls and a lighter graphics build.
An ad network picks banner sizes that fit mobile or desktop, and filters traffic whose claimed browser does not match its hints.
A store shows a link to its Android app on Android and its iPhone app on iOS using the platform hint.
A dashboard counts visits by browser brand and system without relying on the old, hard to read string.
A login system notes the brand and platform of a trusted device, and flags a sudden change as suspicious.
A developer decides which older browsers to still support by reading hint counts from live traffic.

technical_bounds: Platform string quantized, GREASE brand randomizes order
Firefox and Safari do not send it

value.abuse: Browser and OS identification

platform.api: Sec-CH-UA, Sec-CH-UA-Mobile, Sec-CH-UA-Platform request headers; navigator.userAgentData

capabilities.name: Sec-Fetch-* request metadata
capabilities.plain: Browsers add headers saying where a request came from and why, which servers use to block cross-site abuse.
capabilities.meaning: Sec-Fetch-Site, Mode, Dest and User tell the server if a request is same-origin, a navigation, or user triggered. They are not user identifying but help servers tell real browsers from scripts.

limits.headline: Can tell why a request was sent, such as a click or a script
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser adds it to every request automatically
can: See whether a request came from the same site, another site, or from you directly
See whether it came from a click, a typed address or a page script
Block suspicious cross site requests and bots that lack the right labels
cannot: See your name, location or account from these labels
Be changed by the page, since the browser sets them
Tell which person you are
Learn which other pages you visited

story.what_it_is: Browsers label each request with where it came from and why, so servers can reject cross site abuse.

marketing.name: Fetch Metadata
marketing.pitch: Servers can use these labels to block requests that are not meant for them, as a defence against many web attacks.

story.for_you: You never see these labels, but they help protect you. They let sites refuse a request that a hostile page secretly sent using your logged in session.
story.for_makers: Makers add a short rule on the server: only accept some requests from their own pages. It blocks forged requests and data leaks across sites. Because browsers set the labels, a page cannot fake them.

use_cases.example: A bank's server refuses a money transfer sent by another site, because the label says it came from a different site and was not a normal navigation.
A social site only returns private profile data to requests from its own pages, so other sites cannot read it through hidden calls.
A browser game's account server rejects score submissions that do not come from its own game page, which cuts simple cheating by third party scripts.
A web editor such as Google Docs protects document data so other sites cannot load it into a hidden frame.
A streaming site blocks other sites from embedding its video files by checking the destination label.
An engineer adds a middleware that drops cross site requests to private APIs, then watches the logs for blocked probes.
A security team uses the labels to spot probing from a malicious page in the access logs.

technical_bounds: Absent from non-browser clients, making them a bot signal
Cannot be set by page script

value.legit_uses: CSRF and XSSI defense (resource isolation policies)
value.abuse: Bot detection

capabilities.name: TCP/IP passive OS fingerprint (p0f, JA4T)
capabilities.plain: The TCP handshake reveals the operating system through TTL, window size, MSS and option order.
capabilities.meaning: p0f (Zalewski) and JA4T read SYN fields: initial TTL (64 or 128), window size, MSS, window scale and option order. Windows, Linux, iOS and macOS differ, and a mismatch with the User-Agent signals spoofing or a proxy.

limits.headline: Can guess your operating system from how your device opens a connection
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when your device first connects to the server
can: Guess whether you run Windows, Mac, Linux, Android or iPhone from connection details
Catch visitors whose claimed system does not match their real one
Filter attack traffic that has odd connection patterns
cannot: See your name, account or files
Tell the exact version or device model
Be hidden by clearing cookies or using private browsing
Work well through a proxy or relay, since it only sees the last hop

story.what_it_is: The very first network packets from your device reveal what kind of operating system it runs.
story.for_you: You never see it. Every device opens a connection in a slightly different way. A server can read that pattern and guess if you are on Windows, Mac, Linux or a phone.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to catch visitors who say one thing and are another, such as a bot claiming to be an iPhone while running on Linux. It needs no code in the browser and cannot be changed by a page.

use_cases.example: A ticket site sees a visitor claiming to be an iPhone, but the connection pattern looks like a Linux server. It blocks the request as a bot.
An ad fraud service compares the claimed device with the network pattern and drops mismatches from billing.
A browser game blocks sign ups from servers pretending to be Windows players, which stops bot farms and cheat tools.
A bank compares the system seen at login with the customer's usual one and asks for more proof if it changes.
A traffic report separates real phone visits from automated ones that spoof phone browsers.
A firewall flags an unexpected system type on a company login and steps up checks.
A retailer ties repeated suspicious orders to the same network pattern, and slows them for review.

technical_bounds: Altered by load balancers, VPNs and proxies
Reveals the network stack, not the browser

value.legit_uses: OS vs User-Agent mismatch detection, DDoS filtering
value.abuse: Silent OS identification

platform.api: SYN packet capture (p0f v3, JA4T, Zeek)

capabilities.name: TLS session resumption tracking
capabilities.plain: Reuse of a TLS session ticket can link a visitor's connections across sites that share a server.
capabilities.meaning: A session ticket or PSK is a stable ID, so two domains behind one CDN or server can see the same resumption. Sy et al. (ACSAC 2018) found browsers reusing tickets across origins. Chrome partitioned TLS session caches by network isolation key.

limits.headline: Can link your visits across sites on one server if your browser reuses a ticket
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you return to a site and the connection resumes
can: See the same resume ticket when you visit two sites behind one server or content network
Use the ticket as a temporary ID to connect those visits
Speed up your next connection, which is the real purpose
cannot: Link visits on servers that do not share infrastructure
Keep the link for long, since tickets expire in hours or days
Work against browsers that keep separate tickets per site, such as Chrome and Firefox
See your name or what you do on the site
limits.differs: Chrome and Firefox keep tickets separate per site. Safari is partly protected. Older tests showed browsers reusing tickets across sites.

story.what_it_is: Reusing a saved secure connection ticket can link your visits across sites that share a server.
story.for_you: You never see it. To start faster, your browser reuses a ticket from an earlier secure connection. A server that sees the same ticket from two places can tell they are the same browser.
story.for_makers: Makers who run many sites on one server or provider can link visits without cookies. It is a quiet side effect of speed tricks. Browsers cut it by limiting how long tickets live and by splitting them per site.

use_cases.example: A big ad and content network serving many sites sees the same ticket on each. It joins the visits into one profile even with cookies blocked.
A hosting provider counts a returning visitor across all customer sites using the same ticket.
A defence service ties a bot's repeated requests to one ticket and blocks it, even if the address changes.
A video platform links a viewer across its sites and its player embeds through one reused connection.
A game portal hosting many titles on one server links a player's visits across games without a login.
A share button provider sees the same ticket on every site that embeds its button.
A privacy researcher tests whether a browser reuses tickets across sites, to see if it leaks.

technical_bounds: Ticket lifetime limited by browser (about 24 hours to 7 days)
Cross-site linking blocked by partitioning

value.abuse: Cross-domain linkage behind shared infrastructure

history.change: Sy et al. Tracking Users across the Web via TLS Session Resumption (ACSAC 2018)
TLS session cache partitioned with Network Isolation Key

refs.label: Sy et al., Tracking Users across the Web via TLS Session Resumption (ACSAC 2018)

platform.api: TLS 1.2 session tickets, TLS 1.3 PSK; session ID

capabilities.name: VPN, proxy and Tor detection
capabilities.plain: Sites guess whether the visitor hides behind a VPN, proxy or Tor.
capabilities.meaning: Methods: IP lists (Tor exit list, hosting ASNs), latency versus claimed geography, timezone and language versus IP, WebRTC leaks, open ports, MTU and TCP quirks. Residential VPN IPs often slip through.

fields.name: is_vpn
fields.precision: vendor score, false positives about 1 to 10%

limits.headline: Can guess whether you are hiding behind a VPN, proxy or Tor, but not always correctly
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you load a page, sign in, or watch video
can: Check your address against lists of VPN, hosting and Tor addresses
Compare your timezone and language with where your address seems to be
Spot slow response times that suggest a faraway server
Block or challenge you, or show a different catalog
cannot: Be sure when you use a home internet VPN address, which often slips through
Learn your real address if the VPN holds up
See your name or account from detection alone
Avoid wrongly flagging people who use privacy tools for safety

story.what_it_is: Sites guess if you are hiding behind a VPN, proxy or Tor, using address lists and timing clues.
story.for_you: You may see a block page, a missing video or extra checks, and no clear reason. The site thinks your address belongs to a VPN, a data center or Tor, so it treats you with caution.
story.for_makers: Makers buy lists of VPN, proxy and Tor addresses to enforce region rules, stop fraud and slow bots. It is a blunt tool. It also catches honest people who use a VPN for privacy.

use_cases.example: Streaming sites such as Netflix and BBC iPlayer block known VPN addresses to enforce regional licenses, so a viewer abroad sees a proxy error.
A game's store checks for VPN use at purchase to stop regional price tricks, and may ask for a card from the local country.
A bank asks for extra proof when a login arrives from Tor or a known proxy, which may lock out a traveler.
A checkout page scores VPN traffic as higher risk and holds the first order for review.
An ad network refuses to bill clicks from data center and proxy addresses, because they are mostly bots.
A social site restricts new accounts from Tor to slow spam, though a journalist in a risky country may need Tor.
A ticket queue blocks proxy addresses so one buyer cannot hold many places in line.

technical_bounds: False positives on corporate and school networks
Residential proxies and private relays are hard to flag

value.abuse: Blocking privacy users, discrimination

platform.api: IP reputation; Tor bulk exit list; RTT triangulation; timezone mismatch

steps: Compare IP geo with timezone and Accept-Language
Measure latency and run WebRTC probe

capabilities.name: WebRTC ICE host candidates (mDNS)
capabilities.plain: WebRTC used to expose the device's local network IP; browsers now hide it behind a random .local name.
capabilities.meaning: RTCPeerConnection gathers ICE host candidates. Since 2019 and 2020 Chrome and Firefox replace private IPs with mDNS .local names, but granting getUserMedia (camera or microphone) restores real addresses.

fields.name: host candidate
fields.precision: hidden by default in modern browsers

limits.headline: Can try to find your device's home network address, but browsers now hide it
limits.user_action: You join a video call or visit a site that sets up a call connection
can: Start a call connection that lists your device's network addresses
See a random .local name in place of your real home network address in Chrome and Firefox
See your real home network address if you have also allowed camera or microphone
cannot: See your real home network address by default in Chrome and Firefox since 2019 and 2020
Set this up without a site script running
See other devices on your network from this alone
Be sure to bypass a VPN, since modern browsers mask the address
limits.differs: Chrome and Firefox hide the address by default. Safari asks differently and also shows a masked name unless camera or microphone is allowed.

story.what_it_is: Video call tech used to show your device's home network address. Browsers now hide it behind a random name.

marketing.name: mDNS ICE candidates
marketing.pitch: Browsers swap your local address for a random .local name, so calls still connect but the real address stays private.

story.for_you: On a video call or a multiplayer game you notice nothing. Behind the scenes your browser offers a random name instead of your home network address. Calls still work.
story.for_makers: Makers need these candidate addresses to link two devices directly, which cuts server cost and delay. Hiding the real address stops sites from quietly reading it, but direct links on the same network still work.

A game portal hides its ad partner behind a subdomain so ads and player tracking are not blocked.
A privacy researcher uses DNS lookups to spot a hidden tracker behind a friendly sounding subdomain.

story.what_it_is: Ad companies swap IDs through quick redirects so each can recognise the same person.
story.for_you: You never see it. When you load a page, your browser is sent through several ad companies in a blink. Each one passes along its ID for you, so they can all say that they know you.
story.for_makers: Real time ad auctions need every bidder to know who is on the page. Syncing lets them match their private IDs with each other. The result is a web of IDs that makes ads follow people, and a large share of sites take part.

use_cases.example: A news page loads, and a dozen ad companies swap IDs so they can bid on you within 100 milliseconds.
A measurement company uses synced IDs to count people who saw an ad on one site and bought on another.
A free browser game loads ads through partners that sync IDs so bidders value a player more.
A video site sells ad space with synced IDs, which raises the price for known viewers.
A shopper's cart visit is shared through synced IDs so a related ad shows on a news site.
Researchers studied syncing to show how many sites share one ID.

story.for_makers: Tag managers use it to label traffic as search, social or ads. Analytics and ad scripts use it for attribution. Because any script can read it, it is also a leak path for details of the page you were on before.

A shop sees you came from a price comparison site and shows a better coupon.

A paywall that checks if you came from a search engine, and lets you read a free article.

A shop sees which Google ad made each sale, using the _gcl cookies and click IDs.

A retailer builds a remarketing list of people who looked at a product.
A news site measures which stories keep readers longest, to decide what to write.

story.what_it_is: A coded record of your privacy choices that ad companies read before they use your data.

marketing.name: Global Privacy Platform
marketing.pitch: The industry group says GPP carries privacy choices for many regions in one standard string for ad vendors.

story.for_you: You click a cookie or privacy banner. Behind the scenes, the choice becomes a short code that is passed to ad partners. You do not see it, but it should stop them from selling your data if you said no.
story.for_makers: Rules in US states and other regions now differ. One shared string saves ad vendors from building many different signals. It also gives regulators a way to check what the vendor knew.

use_cases.example: A news site records that a Colorado visitor opted out. Each ad bidder reads the GPP string and skips targeting.
A consent tool writes GPP on page load, and the tag manager reads it to block ad tags.
A free browser game site shows an ad auction that respects GPP for players in California and Virginia.
A video site passes GPP into the ad request, so streaming ads follow the viewer's choice.
A retailer uses GPP to decide if it can share purchase data with ad partners for a given state.
A privacy team keeps a log of GPP strings to prove it honored choices if audited.

story.for_you: You never see it. As you move your mouse, click and scroll, a script logs it. The site owner later sees a red and blue picture of the page that shows which parts got attention.
story.for_makers: Design teams want to see why people do not click a button or never see a offer. Heatmaps show scroll depth and rage clicks. The same events often feed session replay, so they tie to a visitor ID.

A browser game site sees where players click on its menu, and fixes the Play button that people miss.
A news site sees that readers stop at 40 percent of an article and puts the subscribe box earlier.
A software firm sees that people click a non-clickable image on the pricing page and makes it a link.
An advertiser sees which part of a landing page draws clicks, then rewrites the headline.
Rage clicks on a menu show that keyboard and screen reader users get stuck, and the team fixes it.

Aggregated views anonymise single users
Mouse movement is off on touch

A streaming service uses a login email token to match viewers to ads on TV and phones.
A game portal with logins sends a token so ad buyers can reach the same player on web and mobile.
An advertiser measures reach across publishers using one ID, instead of counting the same person twice.
A retailer matches its customer list to an ID graph, to find them on other sites.
People can opt out on the vendor site, but few know of it.

story.what_it_is: Sites and ad firms link your visits and devices by their shared IP address.
story.for_you: You never see it. Every site you visit sees your IP address, which shows your city and internet provider. Your phone and laptop on the same Wi-Fi can look like one household.
story.for_makers: IP needs no cookie and no consent box. Matched with device clues, it links phone and laptop. A VPN, Private Relay or shared mobile network can break the link.

use_cases.example: An ad system shows a TV ad on your phone after you searched on your laptop on the same Wi-Fi.
A site counts a visit by city and internet provider, with no cookie at all.
A bank flags a login from a new country or a known VPN address and asks for extra proof.
A multiplayer web game matches you with nearby players, and bans cheaters by IP.
A streaming site blocks videos by country, using the IP to place you.
A shop shows prices in your currency and local stores, based on IP.

technical_bounds: Shared by many people behind NAT
IPv6 privacy addresses rotate daily
iCloud Private Relay and VPNs hide it

marketing.name: IP Protection
marketing.pitch: Chrome pitched it as routing tracker traffic through proxies so sites would not see your real IP address.

story.for_makers: Chrome planned two proxy hops so a tracker would see a proxy address. It would have hurt ad fraud checks and country rules, and Google dropped it in 2025. Makers can still count on IP for location and abuse checks.

A bank would have seen only a proxy address, which makes its fraud and country checks harder.
A multiplayer game keeps banning cheaters by IP, which a proxy would have made harder.

use_cases.example: A news site caches pages so you can read offline on a plane.
A browser game caches its files, so it starts in a second the next time and works offline.
A web editor like Google Docs keeps its code locally so it opens fast and works offline.
A store caches its catalog so browsing feels instant on a weak signal.
An ad or tracking script installs a helper to survive cookie clearing and measure visits later.
A web chat uses a helper to receive push messages when the tab is closed.
A malicious site installs a helper that keeps showing spam alerts after you leave.

technical_bounds: Idle termination about 30 s, single event up to about 5 min (Chrome)
HTTPS only
Same origin scope
Safari 7 day cap on registrations without user visit
Cleared by Clear site data

abuse: Persistent hidden request interception, tracker caching

history.change: ITP 7 day storage cap covers registrations

access.persistence: Registration persists with no fixed expiry. Script checked for update at most every 24 hours. Idle stop after about 30 s (Chrome)
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

capabilities.name: Session replay
capabilities.plain: A script records page changes, mouse, scroll and typing so staff can replay a visit like a video.
capabilities.meaning: Shows exactly what the person saw and did, including text typed in forms unless masked. A 2017 Princeton study found replay scripts on 482 of the top 50,000 sites leaking data. In 2022 to 2025 US wiretap suits grew.

limits.headline: Can record your clicks, scrolls and typing on a page so staff can replay it
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as you use a page with a replay script
can: Record page changes, mouse moves, clicks and scrolls
Record what you type, unless fields are masked
Let staff replay your visit like a video
cannot: Record other sites, tabs or apps
Show fields the site has masked, such as passwords and card numbers
Work if a tracker blocker stops the script
Name you unless the site links it to a login
limits.reach_label: Your whole visit on that site

story.what_it_is: A script records your mouse, clicks and typing so staff can replay your visit like a video.
story.for_you: You never see it. While you use a site, a script records page changes, mouse, scroll and keys. Staff may later watch your visit. It can capture text you type unless the site masks it.
story.for_makers: Teams watch real visits to find bugs and confusing screens. Replay shows what a person saw. It has also brought privacy suits, because replay scripts can capture personal data.

use_cases.example: A shop watches a replay of a checkout that failed, and finds a button that did not work on phones.
A browser game studio replays a stuck player session to find a bug in the menu.
An engineer watches the last 30 seconds before a crash to reproduce a bug.
A bank watches how people fill a loan form, with the number fields masked.
A support team opens a replay of a customer's session to see what went wrong.
A fraud team watches replay for a login session that looks scripted.

technical_bounds: Masks password and payment fields by default in most tools
Needs vendor script on page (blocked by many tools)
Cross-origin iframes need their own script
Consent required in EU and under California wiretap suits

abuse: Capturing typed text, emails and health data

history.change: Princeton: 482 of the top 50,000 sites used replay scripts

refs.label: No boundaries: session replay scripts (Freedom to Tinker 2017)

platform.api: MutationObserver, mouse, scroll and input event listeners sending to vendor

access.persistence: Vendor retention often 30 days to 13 months
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

capabilities.name: Shared Storage API (retired)
capabilities.plain: Cross-site storage whose values could only be read in a locked worker. Retired Oct 2025.
capabilities.meaning: Let scripts write cross-site values (for example a frequency count) and read them only inside a worklet that output through limited channels (selectURL, Private Aggregation). Disabled starting build 153.0.8001.0; code removal follows.

data.metric: Key/value pairs readable in worklet only

limits.headline: Can't store cross site data for ads in Chrome anymore, since it was retired in 2025
limits.user_action: Nothing. It used to happen in the background on pages with embedded ads
can: Have stored values in the browser that any site could use through a locked worker
Have helped choose an ad or count reach without naming you
cannot: Run in Chrome after retirement
Work in Edge, Firefox or Safari
Show stored values to the page directly
Replace cookies for all ad needs

story.what_it_is: Chrome storage that held cross site values in a locked room. Retired.

marketing.name: Shared Storage API
marketing.pitch: Chrome pitched it as unpartitioned storage that could be read only in a locked worklet with limited outputs.

story.for_you: You never saw it. A script could write a value, such as a count, that other sites could read only inside a locked worker. Chrome is turning it off. You will not meet it.
story.for_makers: It was meant to help with things like frequency capping and A/B tests without tracking. Reads had to go through limited paths. With the Privacy Sandbox ad parts retired, it is going away.

use_cases.example: An ad network counted how many times you saw an ad across sites to avoid showing it too often.
A test tool used it to keep the same A or B design across sites you visit.
A game studio could cap how often it showed the same promo across sites.
A publisher used it to pick which ad creative to show without a profile.
A retailer used it to know a visitor saw a sale ad on a partner site.
A social login widget could have stored a flag across sites, read only in a safe room.

technical_bounds: Reads only inside a worklet
selectURL leaks log2(n) bits capped at about 12 bits per 24 hours per top-level site (budget)
No direct script access to values
Chrome only

history.change: Retirement announced (Private Aggregation including Shared Storage)
Disabled from 153.0.8001.0, code removal without staged rollout (post dated Sep 30 2026)

Privacy Sandbox history and removal timeline (checked Oct 2, 2026)

access.persistence: Entries expire after 30 days, renewable on write
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

capabilities.name: Speculation Rules prefetch and prerender
capabilities.plain: A page can load a likely next page early, so a site may see a request before the person visits.
capabilities.meaning: Prefetch or prerender makes the destination server log a hit, and run scripts, before any click, sending Sec-Purpose: prefetch;prerender. Analytics can over count; cookies from a prefetched response apply only on activation.

limits.headline: Can load a likely next page early, so a site may see a visit first
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page guesses where you will go next
can: Load a likely next page before you click
Show the next page almost instantly when you click
Let the next site see a request before you visit
cannot: Run in Firefox or Safari
Run when Chrome's data saver is on or the connection is poor
Show you the page until you click, or count it as a visit in some tools
Load pages from a different site without extra signals
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Samsung Internet support it. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: A page can load a likely next page early, so a site may see a visit before you click.

marketing.name: Prerender pages
marketing.pitch: Chrome says speculation rules can load pages ahead of time so the next click feels instant.

story.for_you: You click a link and the next page appears almost at once. Behind the scenes, the browser loaded it before you clicked. The site may log a hit even if you never open it.
story.for_makers: Instant page loads raise sales and reading time. But prefetching makes the server count a visit early and can run scripts before you arrive. Analytics must wait for activation to avoid inflated numbers.

use_cases.example: A shop prerenders the product page you are likely to open, so checkout feels fast.
A news site prefetches the next article so it opens instantly.
A game portal prefetches the page of the game you hover over, so it loads in a blink.
A tool must ignore hits from prefetched pages, or visit counts go up.
An ad system waits for activation before it counts an impression.
A search result page prerenders the top result so it opens at once.

risks: Server sees visits you never made

technical_bounds: Same-site prefetch carries cookies; cross-origin uses an isolated session without them
Not done when Data Saver or Save-Data is on, or in low memory
Chrome limits concurrent prefetch and prerender counts

abuse: Phantom page views, privacy leak of intent before click

history.change: Prerender2 shipped for omnibox and speculation rules

access.persistence: Prefetch cache about 5 minutes in Chrome
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

safari.note: Not supported at time of research, verify

capabilities.name: Storage Access API
capabilities.plain: Lets an embedded frame ask to use its third-party cookies; the browser may prompt or auto-allow.
capabilities.meaning: Used by embedded SSO, comments and video frames to regain cross-site cookies on Safari, Firefox and Chrome. Safari prompts per embed; Firefox auto-grants after 5 prior interactions and a prompt in other cases; Chrome shows a prompt.

limits.headline: Can ask to use its own cookies when embedded in another site
limits.user_action: You click a button in an embed, such as a login or comment box, and see a prompt
can: Ask the browser to let an embedded frame use its own cookies
Keep you signed in to that embedded service
Get approved without a prompt in some cases, based on past use
cannot: Use the cookies without approval from the browser or you
Reach cookies of other sites
Work if you click Don't allow
Persist forever, since browsers can ask again
limits.differs: Safari and Firefox show a prompt or approve automatically after use. Chrome allows it with less friction.

story.what_it_is: Lets an embedded frame ask to use its cookies from other sites, and the browser may prompt you.

marketing.name: Storage Access API
marketing.pitch: WebKit introduced it as a way for embedded content to ask for cookie access with the person's consent.

story.for_you: You see a prompt in some browsers: this site wants to use cookies on another site. If you allow it, an embedded login, comment box or video frame can recognise you. In some browsers, it grants after some use.
story.for_makers: Single sign on, comments and paid video frames need cookies from their own domain. The API gives them a way back in after blocking. It also gives the browser a place to ask the person, as a check on trackers.

use_cases.example: A comment box from a social site recognises you inside a news article, and lets you post.
A paid video embed checks your subscription cookie from its own domain, so it can play for you.
A game inside a portal frame uses its cookie to remember your login and progress.
A work tool embedded in another app uses its login cookie in the frame.
A payment frame recognises your saved card details, from its own domain.
Browsers use the prompt to stop trackers hidden in embeds from asking for cookies for free.

risks: Prompt can be clicked without thinking

technical_bounds: Needs a user gesture in the iframe
Frame must have interacted as first party in the past (Safari, Firefox)
Sandboxed frames need allow-storage-access-by-user-activation

abuse: Embedded tracker regaining cookies after prompt fatigue

refs.label: Privacy Sandbox status: Storage Access continues

access.prompt_ui: Browser prompt: allow site to use cookies and data on this site
access.persistence: Chrome grant lasts 30 days for the embed; Safari 24 hours of use then reprompt (approx.); Firefox 30 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings
access.iframe: Granted per embedded frame; sandbox needs allow-storage-access-by-user-activation

capabilities.name: IAB TCF consent string
capabilities.plain: A coded record of which ad vendors and purposes the person agreed to in the EU consent banner.
capabilities.meaning: Stored in the euconsent-v2 cookie and read through __tcfapi. TCF v2.3 requires the disclosedVendors segment, and strings without it were invalid from Feb 28 2026. Consent is valid for up to 13 months.

limits.headline: Can see which ad vendors you agreed to in the EU cookie banner
limits.user_action: You tap Accept, Reject, or Manage choices on a cookie banner
can: Check which ad vendors and purposes you said yes to
Pass your choices along to the ad partners it works with
Remember your answer for up to 13 months
Show the banner again if the record is missing or out of date
cannot: Count a choice you never made as your consent
Use a record that lacks the vendor list; since Feb 28 2026 those strings are invalid
Keep your choices past 13 months without asking again
Tell vendors you agreed when you picked Reject all
limits.reach_label: Only choices you made in the banner

story.what_it_is: A saved note of which ad companies and purposes you said yes or no to on a cookie banner.

marketing.name: Transparency and Consent Framework
marketing.pitch: The industry standard that lets sites, ad vendors and consent banners share one record of what a person agreed to.

story.for_you: You see it as the cookie banner in Europe, with a button to accept, reject or manage choices. After you tap, the site stores a coded note of your answers. Ad companies on the page read that note instead of asking you again.
story.for_makers: Publishers and ad vendors need proof that a person agreed before personal data is used for ads. The string travels with every ad request, so each buyer knows what it may do. It also keeps a paper trail for regulators.

use_cases.example: A European newspaper shows a banner, then passes your choices to every ad vendor on the page so only allowed ones load.
In a real-time ad auction, the exchange reads the string first and drops bidders that were not approved.
A free browser games portal shows a consent banner on first visit and only runs personalised ads between rounds if you agreed.
A streaming site plays a generic pre-roll ad instead of a targeted one when you reject the banner.
A measurement tag waits for the consent note before it fires, so rejected visitors are not counted individually.
A web shop only loads retargeting pixels from vendors you ticked, so you do not see its ads follow you around.
A compliance team keeps logs of consent strings to show a regulator that a visitor really said yes.

risks: Consent claims that regulators have challenged

technical_bounds: Covers 11 purposes and 3 special purposes plus vendor IDs
Needs a registered CMP
Not a legal proof by itself

abuse: Weak consent flows (CNIL and Belgian DPA rulings on TCF)

history.change: TCF v2.2 removed legitimate interest for some purposes
TCF v2.3 with disclosedVendors mandatory from Feb 28 2026

access.persistence: euconsent-v2 cookie up to 13 months
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

capabilities.name: Third-party cookies by browser (Nov 2026)
capabilities.plain: Whether an embedded site can set and read its own cookies on other sites, which varies by browser.
capabilities.meaning: Third-party cookies are how ad networks recognise the same person across sites. Safari blocks them, Firefox partitions them, Brave blocks them, Chrome leaves them on by default (user choice) and blocks them in Incognito.

data.metric: Cookie jar per top-level site (partitioned) or global

limits.headline: Can recognise you across sites with embedded cookies, unless your browser blocks them
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when a page with ads or embeds loads
can: Set and later see its own cookie from inside a page on another site
Link your visits across the sites that embed it
Keep working in Chrome, where these cookies stay on by default
Ask the browser for access if it was blocked (Storage Access prompt)
cannot: Set these cookies in Safari, which blocks them
Share one cookie across sites in Firefox, which keeps a separate jar per site
Use them in Incognito windows in Chrome
Get through in Brave, which blocks them
limits.differs: Safari and Brave block them, Firefox splits them per site, and Chrome allows them by default but blocks them in Incognito.

story.what_it_is: Whether an embedded site can store cookies on other sites, which depends on which browser you use.

marketing.name: Intelligent Tracking Prevention
marketing.pitch: Safari blocks cross-site tracking by default so websites cannot follow you from site to site.

marketing.name: Enhanced Tracking Protection
marketing.pitch: Firefox keeps each site's cookies in a separate jar so trackers cannot connect your visits.

marketing.name: Privacy Sandbox
marketing.pitch: Chrome kept third-party cookies and gives people a choice, while offering newer ad tools as alternatives.

story.for_you: You never see these cookies, but they decide whether an ad for boots follows you from a shoe shop to a news site. In Safari and Firefox it mostly cannot. In Chrome it still can, unless you turn it off in settings.
story.for_makers: Ad networks use these cookies to recognise the same person across sites for targeting, frequency caps and conversion counting. Sites also use them for legitimate embeds like logins and payments. When a browser blocks them, makers must switch to first-party data or new APIs.

use_cases.example: A retailer's ad network sets a cookie when you view boots, then recognises you on a recipe blog and shows the same boots.
A Like or Share button embedded on a news article recognises your logged-in account and counts the visit.
An embedded video on a blog remembers your player settings and view history through the video host's own cookie.
A browser game embedded in a portal page saves your progress under the game host's cookie, which breaks when the browser blocks it.
A card check inside a frame on a shop page relies on the bank's cookie to recognise a trusted device.
A bot defence service sets one cookie across many customer sites to spot a scraper hopping between them.
A marketing platform ties an ad click on one site to a purchase on another to report which campaign worked.

risks: Settings differ by browser, so protection is uneven

technical_bounds: Safari: blocked for all, no exceptions except Storage Access API
Firefox: Total Cookie Protection partitions per top-level site by default (June 2022, Firefox 103)
Chrome: kept on by default; no deprecation prompt after the April 2025 decision; Incognito blocks by default
Edge: Tracking Prevention blocks classified trackers, not all

legit_uses: Embedded video, chat, SSO, payment frames
abuse: Cross-site profile building by ad networks

history.change: Total Cookie Protection default for all users
1% of Chrome users had third-party cookies restricted (testing)
Google proposed user choice instead of deprecation
Google confirmed no standalone prompt; users keep the Settings choice
Oct 17: Google retired most remaining Privacy Sandbox APIs; third-party cookies stay

platform.api: document.cookie in iframes; Set-Cookie with SameSite=None; Secure; Storage Access API

access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

samsung.note: Allowed by default, Smart Anti-Tracking blocks some

capabilities.name: Topics API (retired)

capabilities.meaning: Gave ad scripts up to 3 coarse interest topics (one per recent week) from the browsing history of sites that called it. Taxonomy had 469 topics in v2; 5% of results were random noise. Removal rolling out from Chrome 153.

limits.user_action: Nothing. It used to run when an ad script loaded in Chrome
can: Still work in some older Chrome versions until removal rolls out from Chrome 153
Hand ad scripts up to 3 broad interest topics, one per recent week
cannot: Run in Safari, Firefox, or Edge
Give exact sites you visited; it shared broad topics only, and 5% were random noise
Keep working after Chrome finishes removing it
Pick topics from sites that never used the feature

story.what_it_is: Chrome's retired feature that told ad scripts a few broad interests, like Sports or Travel.

marketing.name: Topics API
marketing.pitch: Chrome described it as a way to show relevant ads using broad topics instead of tracking you across sites.

story.for_you: You may have seen an Ad topics switch in Chrome settings. Chrome noted a few broad interests from the sites you visit and shared them with ad scripts. This was being removed in 2026, so most people will never meet it.
story.for_makers: Ad companies wanted a replacement for cookies that still let them pick a relevant ad. Topics gave a coarse interest label with no name or ID attached. Few buyers adopted it, which is part of why it was dropped.

use_cases.example: An ad tech script on a news page asks Chrome for your topics and picks a travel ad because Travel was on the list.
A retailer's ad partner favours camping gear ads for visitors whose topics include Outdoors.
A browser games site shows a sports game promo to visitors whose topics include Fitness, without knowing who they are.
A publisher with many logged-out readers lifts ad income by sending topics along with the ad request.
An ad measurement firm compared topic-based ad results with cookie-based results during Chrome's trials.
Ad tech engineers ran Chrome origin trials and tuned their bidding code to use topic labels.

5% random topic noise
Up to 3 topics per call, 1 per epoch
Blocked when third-party cookies are off or user disabled Ad topics
Not shipped in Firefox or Safari; Edge disabled it

capabilities.name: UTM campaign parameters
capabilities.plain: Tags in the link URL that tell the site which campaign, medium and source sent the person.
capabilities.meaning: Lets a site tie a visit to a specific ad, email or post. Five standard keys: utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, utm_content. Stored in first-party cookies by analytics tools for the session or longer.

limits.headline: Can see which ad, email, or post sent you, from tags in the link
limits.user_action: You tap a link that carries campaign tags, such as an ad or email link
can: See the source, medium, and campaign named in the link
Tie your visit to one specific ad, email, or post
Keep that tag in its own cookie for the visit or longer
Count how many people came from each campaign
cannot: See the tags if the link was copied without them
Learn who you are from the tags alone
Follow you to other sites with these tags
Learn what you did before you clicked

story.what_it_is: Little tags added to a link that tell a site which ad, email or post sent you.

marketing.name: Campaign URL builder
marketing.pitch: Google Analytics shows how to add source, medium and campaign tags to links so you can see what drives visits.

story.for_you: You see them as a long tail on a web address, like utm_source=newsletter. Nothing pops up and the page looks the same. The site just learns which link brought you.
story.for_makers: Marketing teams need to know which email, ad or post paid off. The tags are free, work on any site and need no consent banner on their own. They feed dashboards that decide where the next ad budget goes.

use_cases.example: A shoe brand tags each ad so its dashboard shows that the Instagram story brought more buyers than the Google search ad.
A newsletter tags each link so the editor sees which headline readers clicked from the Tuesday email.
A browser game studio tags links on Discord, YouTube and Reddit to learn which place brings players who stay past day one.
A creator adds tags to the link in a bio so a brand can see exactly how many followers visited.
A Black Friday email carries a campaign tag, so the shop ties each order to that email.
A fraud team spots a campaign tag that suddenly brings thousands of fake sign-ups and cuts that source off.
A product team joins the tags with sign-up data to learn which channel brings paying customers.

risks: Links reveal where you came from
Tags can be shared when you copy the link

technical_bounds: Only as accurate as the link author made them
Not stripped by Chrome; Safari and Firefox strip some tracker IDs but leave UTM keys intact
Cannot identify the person alone

abuse: Appending personal data (email, IDs) to links shared widely
